content.introduction: An adjective is a word that describes or modifies a noun or pronoun by giving more information about its quality, quantity, or state. Adjectives make writing more vivid and precise, which is highly valued in CSS essays, PMS answers, and IELTS writing tasks. Correct placement and comparison of adjectives are common areas tested in grammar exams.
content.urduExplanation: Adjective وہ لفظ ہے جو noun یا pronoun کی خصوصیت بیان کرتا ہے، جیسے 'beautiful', 'tall' یا 'three'۔ یہ ہمیں بتاتا ہے کہ کوئی چیز کیسی ہے، کتنی ہے یا کس قسم کی ہے۔ adjectives عام طور پر noun سے پہلے آتے ہیں، جیسے 'a tall building'، لیکن linking verb کے بعد بھی آ سکتے ہیں، جیسے 'the building is tall'۔ comparative اور superlative degrees کا صحیح استعمال جملوں کو مؤثر بناتا ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns, answering questions like which one, what kind, or how many. They typically appear before the noun they describe or after a linking verb as a subject complement. Adjectives have three degrees of comparison: positive (tall), comparative (taller), and superlative (tallest), used to compare two or more things. Some adjectives are descriptive (happy, red), while others indicate quantity (few, many), possession (my, her), or demonstration (this, those). Correct comparative and superlative forms, along with proper word order, are essential for accurate English.

types.name: Descriptive Adjective
types.description: Describes the quality or characteristic of a noun, e.g., beautiful, tall, honest.

types.name: Quantitative Adjective
types.description: Shows the amount or quantity of a noun, e.g., some, many, few, several.

types.name: Demonstrative Adjective
types.description: Points out a specific noun, e.g., this, that, these, those.

types.name: Possessive Adjective
types.description: Shows ownership and is placed before a noun, e.g., my, your, his, their.

types.name: Comparative Adjective
types.description: Compares two things, usually formed with -er or 'more', e.g., faster, more intelligent.

types.name: Superlative Adjective
types.description: Compares three or more things, usually formed with -est or 'most', e.g., fastest, most intelligent.

rules: Most one-syllable adjectives form the comparative with -er and superlative with -est (tall, taller, tallest).
Adjectives with two or more syllables usually use 'more' and 'most' instead of -er/-est (beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful).
Never use both -er/-est and more/most together (avoid 'more taller' or 'most fastest').
Adjectives usually come before the noun they modify, but can follow linking verbs like be, seem, or become.
When multiple adjectives describe one noun, they generally follow the order: opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material (a beautiful small old round brown wooden table).
Some adjectives are irregular in comparison and must be memorized, such as good/better/best and bad/worse/worst.

examples.text: She wore a beautiful red dress to the ceremony.
examples.note: descriptive adjective

examples.text: There are several students waiting outside.
examples.note: quantitative adjective

examples.text: This book belongs to the library.
examples.note: demonstrative adjective

examples.text: My father works as an engineer.
examples.note: possessive adjective

examples.text: Karachi is larger than Multan.
examples.note: comparative adjective

examples.text: Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world.
examples.note: superlative adjective

examples.text: The exam was more difficult than expected.
examples.note: comparative with 'more'

commonMistakes.wrong: This is more better than that one.
commonMistakes.right: This is better than that one.
commonMistakes.note: 'better' is already comparative and should not be combined with 'more'

commonMistakes.wrong: She is the most intelligentest student in class.
commonMistakes.right: She is the most intelligent student in class.
commonMistakes.note: long adjectives use only 'most', not the -est ending as well

commonMistakes.wrong: He bought a wooden beautiful old table.
commonMistakes.right: He bought a beautiful old wooden table.
commonMistakes.note: adjective order should follow opinion, age, then material

commonMistakes.wrong: This exercise is more easy than the last one.
commonMistakes.right: This exercise is easier than the last one.
commonMistakes.note: one-syllable adjectives like 'easy' typically take -er, not 'more'

practice.question: Choose the correct comparative form: 'Islamabad is ___ than Lahore in terms of planning.'
practice.explanation: 'Clean' is a short adjective, so it forms the comparative by adding -er: cleaner.

practice.question: Which sentence uses adjective order correctly?
options: She has a red small bag.
She has a small red bag.
She has a bag small red.
She has a red bag small.
practice.explanation: The correct order places size before color: small red bag.

practice.question: Select the correct superlative form of 'good'.
practice.explanation: 'Good' is irregular, and its superlative form is 'best', not a regular -est or 'most' form.

quiz.question: Choose the sentence with the correct adjective form.
options: This is the most beautifulest garden I have seen.
This is the beautifulest garden I have seen.
This is the most beautiful garden I have seen.
This is more beautiful garden I have seen.
quiz.explanation: Long adjectives like 'beautiful' use 'most' alone for the superlative, without an -est ending.

quiz.question: Which word is a possessive adjective in the sentence: 'Her essay won the competition'?
quiz.explanation: 'Her' shows ownership of the essay and modifies the noun directly, making it a possessive adjective.

quiz.question: Choose the correctly ordered sentence.
options: He bought an old round wooden table.
He bought a wooden old round table.
He bought a round old wooden table.
He bought an old wooden round table.
quiz.explanation: Correct order is age before shape before material: old round wooden table.

content.summary: Adjectives describe or modify nouns and pronouns, showing quality, quantity, or possession, and change form to express comparison. Short adjectives use -er/-est while longer ones use more/most, and irregular forms like good/better/best must be memorized. Correct adjective order and comparison forms are frequently tested and easy to master with practice.

content.introduction: An adverb is a word that modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb by adding information about how, when, where, or to what extent something happens. Adverbs add precision and detail to sentences, which strengthens argumentative writing for CSS and PMS essays and enhances fluency in IELTS speaking. Recognizing adverb types and their correct placement is a key grammar skill tested in most English exams.
content.urduExplanation: Adverb وہ لفظ ہے جو verb، adjective یا کسی دوسرے adverb کے بارے میں مزید معلومات دیتا ہے، جیسے 'quickly', 'very' یا 'yesterday'۔ یہ بتاتا ہے کہ کوئی کام کیسے، کب، کہاں یا کس حد تک ہوا۔ زیادہ تر adverbs adjective میں '-ly' لگا کر بنائے جاتے ہیں، جیسے 'quick' سے 'quickly'۔ صحیح جگہ پر adverb کا استعمال جملے کے معنی کو واضح اور درست بناتا ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Adverbs answer questions such as how, when, where, and to what degree, and they can modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Many adverbs of manner are formed by adding -ly to an adjective (slow becomes slowly), though some adverbs, like fast and well, do not follow this pattern. Adverbs are categorized into manner, time, place, frequency, and degree, each serving a distinct descriptive purpose. Their position in a sentence can shift meaning or emphasis, so correct placement is important, especially with frequency adverbs like always, often, and never, which usually appear before the main verb but after the verb 'to be'.

types.name: Adverb of Manner
types.description: Describes how an action is performed, e.g., quickly, carefully, well.

types.name: Adverb of Time
types.description: Describes when an action happens, e.g., yesterday, now, soon.

types.name: Adverb of Place
types.description: Describes where an action happens, e.g., here, there, outside.

types.name: Adverb of Frequency
types.description: Describes how often an action happens, e.g., always, often, rarely, never.

types.name: Adverb of Degree
types.description: Describes the intensity or extent of an action or quality, e.g., very, quite, almost, too.

rules: Adverbs of manner are usually placed after the main verb or after the object if there is one (She sings beautifully).
Adverbs of frequency are placed before the main verb but after auxiliary verbs and the verb 'to be' (He always arrives on time; She is often late).
Adverbs of time are typically placed at the beginning or end of a sentence, not in the middle (Yesterday, I finished my homework).
Do not confuse adjectives and adverbs; adjectives describe nouns while adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs (She is a careful driver vs. She drives carefully).
Some words ending in -ly, like friendly and lovely, are actually adjectives, not adverbs, so check meaning carefully.
Adverbs of degree usually appear directly before the adjective or adverb they modify (The exam was extremely difficult).

examples.text: She completed the task quickly and efficiently.
examples.note: adverb of manner

examples.text: We will submit the report tomorrow.
examples.note: adverb of time

examples.text: Please wait here until I return.
examples.note: adverb of place

examples.text: He always double-checks his answers before submitting.
examples.note: adverb of frequency

examples.text: The lecture was extremely informative.
examples.note: adverb of degree

examples.text: She speaks English fluently after years of practice.
examples.note: adverb of manner

examples.text: They rarely miss a class during the semester.
examples.note: adverb of frequency

commonMistakes.wrong: She sings beautiful in the choir.
commonMistakes.right: She sings beautifully in the choir.
commonMistakes.note: verbs must be modified by adverbs, not adjectives

commonMistakes.wrong: He drives very careful on the highway.
commonMistakes.right: He drives very carefully on the highway.
commonMistakes.note: the adverb form 'carefully' is needed to modify the verb 'drives'

commonMistakes.wrong: Always he checks his email in the morning.
commonMistakes.right: He always checks his email in the morning.
commonMistakes.note: frequency adverbs are placed before the main verb, not at the start of the sentence

commonMistakes.wrong: She is a friendly speaking person.
commonMistakes.right: She is a friendly, well-spoken person.
commonMistakes.note: 'friendly' is an adjective, not an adverb, despite ending in -ly

practice.question: Choose the sentence with the adverb placed correctly.
options: She studies at night often always.
practice.explanation: Adverbs of frequency like 'often' are placed before the main verb in a simple present sentence.

practice.question: Which word correctly completes: 'He answered the question ___.'?
practice.explanation: 'Confidently' is the adverb form needed to modify the verb 'answered'.

practice.question: Identify the adverb of degree in: 'The test was quite challenging.'
practice.explanation: 'Quite' modifies the adjective 'challenging' by showing its intensity, making it an adverb of degree.

quiz.question: Choose the correctly formed sentence.
options: She is always on time for meetings.
She always is on time for meetings.
Always she is on time for meetings.
She is on time always for meetings.
quiz.explanation: With the verb 'to be', the frequency adverb comes after it: 'is always'.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses an adverb instead of an adjective?
quiz.explanation: 'Perfectly' correctly modifies the verb 'performed', while 'perfect' would incorrectly be used as an adverb.

quiz.question: Identify the adverb of time in: 'We will meet again next week.'
quiz.explanation: 'Next week' tells us when the meeting will happen, making it an adverb of time.

content.summary: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs to express manner, time, place, frequency, or degree. Correct placement, especially for frequency adverbs before the main verb and after 'to be', is essential for natural and accurate English. Always distinguish adverbs from adjectives, since only adverbs can properly modify verbs and other adverbs.

content.introduction: A conjunction is a word that connects words, phrases, or clauses within a sentence, allowing writers to build complex and well-structured ideas. Conjunctions are essential for essay writing in CSS and PMS, where logical flow and connected arguments are heavily rewarded, and for coherence in IELTS writing and speaking. Understanding coordinating, subordinating, and correlative conjunctions helps avoid sentence fragments and run-on sentences.
content.urduExplanation: Conjunction وہ لفظ ہے جو دو الفاظ، phrases یا جملوں کو آپس میں جوڑتا ہے، جیسے 'and', 'but' یا 'because'۔ یہ ہمیں اپنے خیالات کو منطقی انداز میں جوڑنے میں مدد دیتا ہے، جس سے تحریر زیادہ روانی والی اور واضح بنتی ہے۔ coordinating conjunctions برابر حیثیت رکھنے والے جملوں کو جوڑتے ہیں، جبکہ subordinating conjunctions ایک اہم جملے کو دوسرے کم اہم جملے سے جوڑتے ہیں۔ صحیح conjunction کا انتخاب جملے کے معنی کو درست اور واضح بناتا ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Conjunctions link words, phrases, or clauses to show relationships such as addition, contrast, cause, condition, or time. Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet) join elements of equal grammatical rank, while subordinating conjunctions (because, although, if, since, when) join a dependent clause to an independent clause. Correlative conjunctions work in pairs, such as either...or and not only...but also, and require parallel structure on both sides. Using the correct conjunction and punctuation prevents run-on sentences, comma splices, and sentence fragments, which are common errors in exam writing.

types.name: Coordinating Conjunction
types.description: Joins words, phrases, or independent clauses of equal importance, e.g., and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor.

types.name: Subordinating Conjunction
types.description: Joins a dependent clause to an independent clause, showing cause, condition, contrast, or time, e.g., because, although, if, when, since.

types.name: Correlative Conjunction
types.description: Works in pairs to connect balanced words or phrases, e.g., either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, both...and.

rules: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction when it joins two independent clauses (She studied hard, so she passed the exam).
Do not use a comma when a coordinating conjunction joins only two words or phrases, not two full clauses (She studied hard and passed the exam).
Subordinating conjunctions can begin a sentence; when they do, a comma follows the dependent clause (Although it rained, we continued the match).
Correlative conjunctions require parallel grammatical structure on both sides (Not only did she study, but she also revised thoroughly).
Avoid using two conjunctions with the same meaning together (avoid 'Although the exam was hard, but I passed it'; choose one).
Choose the subordinating conjunction that accurately reflects the logical relationship: because (reason), although (contrast), if (condition), when (time).

examples.text: She wanted to travel abroad, but she could not afford it.
examples.note: coordinating conjunction

examples.text: Although he was tired, he finished his assignment.
examples.note: subordinating conjunction

examples.text: Either you submit the form today, or you will miss the deadline.
examples.note: correlative conjunction

examples.text: He studies English and Urdu at the academy.
examples.note: coordinating conjunction (joining words)

examples.text: Because the roads were blocked, the exam was delayed.
examples.note: subordinating conjunction (reason)

examples.text: Not only did she pass, but she also topped the merit list.
examples.note: correlative conjunction

examples.text: We stayed indoors since it was raining heavily.
examples.note: subordinating conjunction (reason)

commonMistakes.wrong: Although she was busy, but she helped her friend.
commonMistakes.right: Although she was busy, she helped her friend.
commonMistakes.note: do not use both 'although' and 'but' together to express the same contrast

commonMistakes.wrong: Neither he nor his friends is coming to the party.
commonMistakes.right: Neither he nor his friends are coming to the party.
commonMistakes.note: the verb agrees with the noun closest to it, here the plural 'friends'

commonMistakes.wrong: She is not only intelligent but also she is hardworking.
commonMistakes.right: She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
commonMistakes.note: correlative conjunctions require parallel structure on both sides

commonMistakes.wrong: I like tea, and coffee I also like.
commonMistakes.right: I like tea, and I also like coffee.
commonMistakes.note: coordinating conjunctions should join clauses in a natural, parallel word order

practice.question: Choose the sentence with correct comma usage.
options: She was tired and, she kept working.
She was tired, and she kept working.
She was tired and she, kept working.
She was tired, and, she kept working.
practice.explanation: A comma is placed before the coordinating conjunction 'and' because it joins two independent clauses.

practice.question: Which sentence uses correlative conjunctions correctly?
options: Both my sister and my brother is studying abroad.
Both my sister and my brother are studying abroad.
Both my sister and brother is study abroad.
Both my sister as well my brother are studying abroad.
practice.explanation: 'Both...and' requires a plural verb, and the sentence must maintain parallel structure.

practice.question: Choose the correct subordinating conjunction: '___ it was raining, the match continued.'
practice.explanation: 'Although' correctly shows contrast between the rain and the match continuing despite it.

quiz.question: Which sentence avoids a redundant conjunction pair?
options: Because he was late, so he missed the bus.
Because he was late, he missed the bus.
Although he was late, so he missed the bus.
Since he was late, so he missed the bus.
quiz.explanation: Using only 'because' avoids the redundant pairing with 'so', which repeats the same logical relationship.

quiz.question: Choose the sentence with correct correlative conjunction agreement.
options: Neither the teacher nor the students was ready.
Neither the teacher nor the students were ready.
Neither the teacher or the students were ready.
Neither the teacher nor students is ready.
quiz.explanation: The verb agrees with 'students', the noun closest to it, requiring the plural verb 'were'.

quiz.question: Which subordinating conjunction best completes: '___ you finish your homework, you cannot watch television.'?
quiz.explanation: 'Unless' correctly expresses the condition needed to allow watching television.

content.summary: Conjunctions connect words, phrases, and clauses to build logical, well-structured sentences, and they fall into coordinating, subordinating, and correlative types. Correct comma placement with coordinating conjunctions and parallel structure with correlative conjunctions are frequently tested points. Avoiding redundant conjunction pairs and matching subject-verb agreement in correlative structures leads to clearer, more accurate writing.

content.introduction: A determiner is a word placed before a noun to clarify what the noun refers to, indicating specificity, quantity, or possession. Determiners include articles, demonstratives, possessives, and quantifiers, and choosing the right one is one of the most common challenges for Urdu-speaking learners of English. Correct use of determiners, especially articles, is heavily tested in CSS, PMS, and IELTS grammar and writing sections.
content.urduExplanation: Determiner وہ لفظ ہے جو noun سے پہلے آ کر یہ واضح کرتا ہے کہ ہم کس چیز، کتنی مقدار یا کس کی ملکیت کی بات کر رہے ہیں، جیسے 'a', 'the', 'this', 'my' یا 'some'۔ چونکہ اردو میں articles (a, an, the) کا کوئی براہ راست متبادل نہیں ہوتا، اس لیے طلبہ کو اکثر یہ استعمال کرنے میں دشواری ہوتی ہے۔ articles کے علاوہ determiners میں demonstratives (this, that)، possessives (my, your) اور quantifiers (some, many, few) شامل ہیں۔ صحیح determiner کا انتخاب جملے کے معنی کو واضح اور درست بناتا ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Determiners are words that come before nouns to specify which one, how many, or whose it is, and they include articles, demonstratives, possessives, and quantifiers. The articles 'a' and 'an' are indefinite, used for non-specific or first-mentioned singular countable nouns, while 'the' is definite, used for specific or previously mentioned nouns. Demonstrative determiners (this, that, these, those) point to specific nouns based on distance or number, and possessive determiners (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) show ownership. Quantifiers such as some, any, much, many, few, and little indicate amount, and the correct choice depends on whether the noun is countable or uncountable.

types.name: Article
types.description: Indicates definiteness or indefiniteness of a noun, e.g., a, an (indefinite) and the (definite).

types.name: Demonstrative Determiner
types.description: Points to specific nouns based on distance and number, e.g., this, that, these, those.

types.name: Possessive Determiner
types.description: Shows ownership before a noun, e.g., my, your, his, her, its, our, their.

types.name: Quantifier
types.description: Indicates the amount or quantity of a noun, e.g., some, any, many, much, few, little, several.

types.name: Numeral Determiner
types.description: Specifies exact number before a noun, e.g., one, two, first, second.

rules: Use 'a' before words beginning with a consonant sound and 'an' before words beginning with a vowel sound (a university, an hour).
Use 'the' when referring to a specific noun already known to the listener or mentioned earlier in the conversation (I bought a pen. The pen is blue.).
Do not use articles before uncountable nouns when speaking generally (Water is essential for life, not The water is essential for life, unless referring to specific water).
Use 'many' and 'few' with countable plural nouns, and 'much' and 'little' with uncountable nouns (many books, much time).
Demonstrative determiners must agree in number with the noun they modify: this/that with singular nouns, these/those with plural nouns.
Possessive determiners are always followed directly by a noun and never stand alone (my book, not my is on the table).

examples.text: She bought a laptop and an umbrella yesterday.
examples.note: indefinite articles

examples.text: The teacher who taught us mathematics has retired.
examples.note: definite article

examples.text: This essay is better than that one.
examples.note: demonstrative determiner

examples.text: Our school won the inter-college competition.
examples.note: possessive determiner

examples.text: There is little time left before the exam.
examples.note: quantifier with uncountable noun

examples.text: Many students applied for the scholarship this year.
examples.note: quantifier with countable noun

examples.text: These books belong to the university library.
examples.note: demonstrative determiner (plural)

commonMistakes.wrong: She is an university student.
commonMistakes.right: She is a university student.
commonMistakes.note: 'university' starts with a consonant sound /j/, so it takes 'a', not 'an'

commonMistakes.wrong: I have much books to read this month.
commonMistakes.right: I have many books to read this month.
commonMistakes.note: 'books' is countable, so it takes 'many', not 'much'

commonMistakes.wrong: The honesty is the best policy.
commonMistakes.right: Honesty is the best policy.
commonMistakes.note: abstract nouns used in general statements do not take 'the'

commonMistakes.wrong: This are my favorite books.
commonMistakes.right: These are my favorite books.
commonMistakes.note: the demonstrative determiner must agree in number with the plural noun 'books'

practice.question: Choose the correct article: 'He is ___ honest man.'
practice.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a silent 'h', producing a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.

practice.question: Select the correct quantifier: 'There isn't ___ sugar left in the jar.'
practice.explanation: 'Sugar' is uncountable, so it correctly pairs with the quantifier 'much'.

practice.question: Choose the correct demonstrative determiner: '___ shoes over there belong to Ahmed.'
practice.explanation: 'Those' agrees with the plural noun 'shoes' and indicates distance ('over there').

quiz.question: Which sentence uses the article correctly?
options: I saw an unicorn in my dream.
I saw a unicorn in my dream.
I saw the unicorn in my dream first time.
I saw unicorn in my dream.
quiz.explanation: 'Unicorn' begins with a consonant sound /j/, so it correctly takes 'a', not 'an'.

quiz.question: Choose the sentence with the correct possessive determiner.
options: The dog wagged it's tail happily.
The dog wagged its tail happily.
The dog wagged their tail happily.
The dog wagged his self tail happily.
quiz.explanation: 'Its' is the correct possessive determiner showing the dog's ownership of the tail, with no apostrophe.

quiz.question: Select the correctly completed sentence: 'There are ___ students absent today.'
quiz.explanation: 'A few' is used with countable plural nouns like 'students' to indicate a small positive number.

content.summary: Determiners, including articles, demonstratives, possessives, and quantifiers, come before nouns to specify identity, ownership, or quantity. Correct article choice (a/an/the) and matching quantifiers to countable or uncountable nouns are the most common problem areas for Urdu-speaking learners. Practicing these patterns closely improves accuracy in both formal exam writing and everyday English.

content.introduction: An interjection is a word or short phrase used to express sudden emotion, such as surprise, joy, pain, or excitement, and it usually stands apart from the rest of the sentence. Interjections are common in spoken English and informal writing, adding natural expressiveness to conversation, which is useful for IELTS speaking fluency. Although rarely tested directly in CSS or PMS grammar sections, understanding interjections helps learners recognize and correctly punctuate expressive language.
content.urduExplanation: Interjection ایک ایسا لفظ یا مختصر جملہ ہے جو اچانک جذبات کا اظہار کرتا ہے، جیسے خوشی، درد، حیرانی یا جوش، مثلاً 'Wow!', 'Ouch!' یا 'Alas!'۔ یہ عام طور پر جملے کے باقی حصے سے الگ ہوتا ہے اور اکثر exclamation mark (!) کے ساتھ استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ interjections زیادہ تر بول چال اور غیر رسمی تحریر میں استعمال ہوتے ہیں تاکہ جذبات کو زیادہ فطری انداز میں ظاہر کیا جا سکے۔
content.englishExplanation: Interjections are short exclamatory words or phrases that express strong or sudden feelings and are grammatically independent from the rest of the sentence. They are typically followed by an exclamation mark when expressing strong emotion, or by a comma when the emotion is mild and part of a longer sentence. Common interjections include Wow, Oh, Alas, Hurray, Ouch, and Well. Because interjections do not perform a grammatical function like other parts of speech, they are mainly used in dialogue, informal writing, and spoken English rather than formal academic writing.
rules: Use an exclamation mark after an interjection that expresses strong emotion (Wow! That is an amazing achievement.).
Use a comma after a mild interjection that is followed by the rest of the sentence (Well, I suppose we should start now.).
Interjections do not have grammatical connections to the rest of the sentence and can be removed without affecting sentence structure.
Avoid using interjections in formal academic writing such as CSS or PMS essays, as they are considered too informal.
Choose an interjection appropriate to the emotion being expressed, since different interjections suit different feelings (Ouch for pain, Alas for sorrow, Hurray for joy).

examples.text: Wow! You scored the highest marks in the class.
examples.note: interjection of surprise

examples.text: Ouch! That really hurt.
examples.note: interjection of pain

examples.text: Alas! The team lost the final match.
examples.note: interjection of sorrow

examples.text: Hurray! We won the debate competition.
examples.note: interjection of joy

examples.text: Well, I guess we should leave now.
examples.note: mild interjection with comma

examples.text: Oh! I did not expect to see you here.
examples.note: interjection of surprise

examples.text: Bravo! That was an excellent performance.
examples.note: interjection of praise

commonMistakes.wrong: Wow you did a great job.
commonMistakes.right: Wow! You did a great job.
commonMistakes.note: a strong interjection needs an exclamation mark to separate it from the sentence

commonMistakes.wrong: Alas, We use interjections frequently in our CSS essay.
commonMistakes.right: We should avoid interjections in formal CSS essays.
commonMistakes.note: interjections are too informal for academic exam writing

commonMistakes.wrong: Ouch. that hurts a lot
commonMistakes.right: Ouch! That hurts a lot.
commonMistakes.note: the sentence following an interjection should start with a capital letter and proper punctuation

commonMistakes.wrong: Well I think we should go now
commonMistakes.right: Well, I think we should go now.
commonMistakes.note: a mild interjection is followed by a comma before the rest of the sentence

practice.question: Which sentence uses an interjection correctly?
practice.explanation: A strong interjection like 'Wow' is followed by an exclamation mark, and the next sentence starts with a capital letter.

practice.question: Choose the interjection that best expresses pain.
practice.explanation: 'Ouch' is the standard interjection used to express sudden physical pain.

practice.question: Which type of writing should generally avoid interjections?
practice.explanation: Interjections are too informal and are avoided in formal academic essays like those for CSS or PMS.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a mild interjection?
options: Well I am not sure about this.
Well, I am not sure about this.
Well! I am not sure about this.
Well; I am not sure about this.
quiz.explanation: A comma is used after a mild interjection like 'well' before continuing with the rest of the sentence.

quiz.question: Choose the interjection that expresses sorrow.
quiz.explanation: 'Alas' is traditionally used to express sadness or regret.

quiz.question: What is a key feature of interjections?
options: They must agree with the subject of the sentence.
They are grammatically independent from the rest of the sentence.
They always require a direct object.
quiz.explanation: Interjections stand apart grammatically and can be removed without changing the sentence's core structure.

content.summary: Interjections are short words or phrases that express sudden emotion and stand grammatically apart from the rest of the sentence. Strong interjections take an exclamation mark, while mild ones are followed by a comma, and both should be avoided in formal academic writing. Recognizing common interjections like Wow, Alas, Ouch, and Hurray helps learners understand expressive spoken and informal English.

content.introduction: A noun is the name of a person, place, animal, thing, substance, or idea.
content.urduExplanation: کسی شخص، جگہ، جانور، چیز، مادے یا خیال کے نام کو اسم یعنی Noun کہتے ہیں۔
content.englishExplanation: The main noun categories in this lesson are proper, common, collective, abstract, countable, uncountable, material, and compound nouns. A noun may belong to more than one category: information is both common and uncountable, while Islamabad is both proper and countable in some contexts. Always judge the noun from its use in the sentence.

types.name: Proper Noun
types.description: A Proper Noun is the special name of a particular person, place, day, country, or institution.
types.urduExplanation: اسمِ خاص کسی خاص شخص، جگہ، دن، ملک یا ادارے کا مخصوص نام ہوتا ہے۔

examples.text: Fatima Jinnah was the sister of Mohammad Ali Jinnah.
examples.urdu: فاطمہ جناح، محمد علی جناح کی بہن تھیں۔
examples.note: Fatima Jinnah and Mohammad Ali Jinnah are specific people, so they are Proper Nouns and begin with capital letters.

examples.text: The Indus River flows through Pakistan.
examples.urdu: دریائے سندھ پاکستان سے ہو کر گزرتا ہے۔
examples.note: Indus River is the specific name of a river, and Pakistan is the specific name of a country; both are Proper Nouns.

examples.text: The Faisal Mosque is beautiful.
examples.urdu: فیصل مسجد خوبصورت ہے۔
examples.note: Faisal Mosque names one particular mosque, so it is a Proper Noun and begins with capital letters.

examples.text: The commission will meet on Monday in Quetta.
examples.urdu: کمیشن پیر کے روز کوئٹہ میں اجلاس کرے گا۔
examples.note: Monday and Quetta are specific names of a day and a place, so both are Proper Nouns.

rules: Always begin a **Proper Noun** with a **capital letter**.
A Proper Noun names one **specific person, place, day, country, or institution**.
Do not use **a** or **an** before most Proper Nouns.

commonMistakes.wrong: I will meet you on monday.
commonMistakes.right: I will meet you on Monday.
commonMistakes.urdu: میں آپ سے پیر کے روز ملوں گا۔
commonMistakes.note: Days and months are Proper Nouns, so they begin with capital letters.

commonMistakes.wrong: I bought a Book yesterday.
commonMistakes.right: I bought a book yesterday.
commonMistakes.urdu: میں نے کل ایک کتاب خریدی۔
commonMistakes.note: Book is a Common Noun here because it does not name one specific book; it should be lowercase.

commonMistakes.wrong: I visited the city Karachi.
commonMistakes.right: I visited Karachi.
commonMistakes.urdu: میں کراچی گیا۔
commonMistakes.note: Karachi already gives the specific city name, so city is unnecessary in ordinary usage. The city of Karachi is also correct when emphasis is needed.

commonMistakes.wrong: A Ali is my friend.
commonMistakes.right: Ali is my friend.
commonMistakes.urdu: علی میرا دوست ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Most Proper Nouns do not take a or an because Ali is already a specific name.

practice.question: Which word is a proper noun in “The students visited Taxila”?
practice.explanation: Taxila is the specific name of a place.

practice.question: Choose the correctly capitalized form.
practice.explanation: The name of the subject is written as Pakistan Studies.

quiz.question: Which is a proper noun in “Ayesha visited Lahore”?
quiz.explanation: Ayesha is a specific name; Lahore is also proper.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form.
quiz.explanation: Pakistan begins with a capital letter.

quiz.question: Which contains only proper nouns?
quiz.explanation: Karachi and Monday are specific names.

quiz.question: Which noun is proper in “The Indus River flows”?
quiz.explanation: Indus River names one particular river.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: CSS is an official abbreviation written in capitals.

types.name: Common Noun
types.description: A Common Noun is a general name given to every person, place, animal, or thing of the same class or kind.
types.urduExplanation: اسمِ عام ایک ہی قسم کے عام شخص، جگہ، جانور یا چیز کے لیے استعمال ہونے والا نام ہے۔

examples.text: A boy is running on the road.
examples.urdu: ایک لڑکا سڑک پر دوڑ رہا ہے۔
examples.note: Boy and road are Common Nouns because they name a general person and place, not specific names.

examples.text: The teacher is in the classroom.
examples.urdu: استاد کلاس روم میں ہے۔
examples.note: Teacher and classroom are Common Nouns. The article the makes these general nouns specific in this context.

examples.text: The student is reading a book.
examples.urdu: طالب علم ایک کتاب پڑھ رہا ہے۔
examples.note: Student and book are Common Nouns. Student is the subject, and book is the object of reading.

examples.text: The river passes through the town.
examples.urdu: دریا قصبے سے گزرتا ہے۔
examples.note: River and town are Common Nouns because they name general kinds of places or things.

rules: A **Common Noun** names a **general person, place, animal, or thing**.
Use **a** or **an** with one **singular countable Common Noun** when needed.
Use **the** when the context makes a Common Noun **specific**.

commonMistakes.wrong: I bought a Book yesterday.
commonMistakes.right: I bought a book yesterday.
commonMistakes.urdu: میں نے کل ایک کتاب خریدی۔
commonMistakes.note: Book is a Common Noun, so it normally begins with a lowercase letter.

commonMistakes.wrong: The Student is reading.
commonMistakes.right: The student is reading.
commonMistakes.urdu: طالب علم پڑھ رہا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Student is a Common Noun. It is not capitalized merely because it follows the article the.

commonMistakes.wrong: I bought book.
commonMistakes.right: I bought a book.
commonMistakes.urdu: میں نے ایک کتاب خریدی۔
commonMistakes.note: A singular countable Common Noun normally needs a determiner such as a, an, the, my, or this.

commonMistakes.wrong: I need a water.
commonMistakes.right: I need some water.
commonMistakes.urdu: مجھے کچھ پانی چاہیے۔
commonMistakes.note: Water is normally an Uncountable Noun, so a or an is not used directly before it.

commonMistakes.wrong: There are many childs in the park.
commonMistakes.right: There are many children in the park.
commonMistakes.urdu: پارک میں بہت سے بچے ہیں۔
commonMistakes.note: Child has the irregular plural form children, not childs.

practice.question: Which word is a common noun in “The officer read the report”?
practice.explanation: Officer is a general name for a person.

practice.question: Choose the correct sentence.
practice.explanation: Book is singular and countable, so it needs a.

quiz.question: Which is common in “The teacher entered”?
quiz.explanation: Teacher is a general name.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: The singular candidate takes works.

quiz.question: Which uses a common noun?
quiz.explanation: Child is a general name.

quiz.question: Choose the correct article.
quiz.explanation: Book is singular and countable.

quiz.question: Which is common in “The doctor examined Ali”?
quiz.explanation: Doctor is a general profession.

ruleExamples: The **book** on the table is mine.

types.name: Collective Noun
types.description: A Collective Noun names a group of people, animals, or things as one unit.
types.urduExplanation: اسمِ مجموعہ لوگوں، جانوروں یا چیزوں کے ایسے گروہ کا نام ہے جسے ایک اکائی سمجھا جائے۔

examples.text: The committee approved the plan.
examples.urdu: کمیٹی نے منصوبے کی منظوری دی۔
examples.note: Committee names a group acting as one unit, so it is a Collective Noun. It takes the singular verb approved in the past tense.

examples.text: The team won the match.
examples.urdu: ٹیم نے میچ جیت لیا۔
examples.note: Team names several people as one group, so it is a Collective Noun. It acts as one unit here.

examples.text: The jury reached a decision.
examples.urdu: جیوری ایک فیصلے پر پہنچی۔
examples.note: Jury names a group of people. It is singular here because the jury reached one decision as a unit.

examples.text: The staff are checking their files.
examples.urdu: عملہ اپنی فائلیں چیک کر رہا ہے۔
examples.note: Staff is a Collective Noun. It takes are here because the members are acting separately.

rules: A **Collective Noun** names a **group** of people, animals, or things.
Use a **singular verb** when the group acts as **one unit**.
A **plural verb** may be used when the **members act separately**.

commonMistakes.wrong: The committee approve the plan.
commonMistakes.right: The committee approves the plan.
commonMistakes.urdu: کمیٹی منصوبے کی منظوری دیتی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Committee acts as one unit here, so the singular verb approves is needed.

commonMistakes.wrong: The team are winning the match.
commonMistakes.right: The team is winning the match.
commonMistakes.urdu: ٹیم میچ جیت رہی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Team is treated as one unit in this sentence, so use is.

commonMistakes.wrong: The jury have reached one decision.
commonMistakes.right: The jury has reached one decision.
commonMistakes.urdu: جیوری ایک فیصلے پر پہنچ چکی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: One decision shows that the jury acts as a single unit, so use has.

practice.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The committee have agreed as one body.
The committee has agreed as one body.
practice.explanation: The committee acts as one unit, so has is correct.

practice.question: Which word is a collective noun?
practice.explanation: Flock names a group of birds.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: Committee acts as one unit.

quiz.question: Which is collective in “The army defended”?
quiz.explanation: Army names a group.

quiz.question: Choose the correct pronoun.
options: The jury announced their decision as one body.
The jury announced its decision as one body.
quiz.explanation: A single group takes its.

quiz.question: Which shows separate action?
options: The team are arguing among themselves.
quiz.explanation: Are shows members acting separately.

quiz.question: Choose the correct verb.
options: The flock of birds is moving south.
The flock of birds are moving souths.
The flock of birds moveing south.
The flock of birds be moving south.
quiz.explanation: Flock is the singular head noun.

ruleExamples: The **family are sitting** in different rooms.

types.name: Abstract Noun
types.description: An Abstract Noun names an idea, quality, feeling, or state that cannot be touched.
types.urduExplanation: اسمِ کیفیت کسی خیال، خوبی، احساس یا حالت کا نام ہے جسے چھوا نہیں جا سکتا۔

examples.text: Honesty builds public trust.
examples.urdu: ایمان داری عوامی اعتماد پیدا کرتی ہے۔
examples.note: Honesty and trust are Abstract Nouns because they name qualities or ideas. Honesty is singular, so the verb is builds.

examples.text: Justice protects citizens.
examples.urdu: انصاف شہریوں کی حفاظت کرتا ہے۔
examples.note: Justice is an Abstract Noun naming an idea. It is singular, so it takes protects.

examples.text: The policy brought hope to families.
examples.urdu: پالیسی خاندانوں کے لیے امید لائی۔
examples.note: Hope is an Abstract Noun naming a feeling. It is the object of brought.

examples.text: Courage helps a candidate face difficulty.
examples.urdu: حوصلہ امیدوار کو مشکل کا سامنا کرنے میں مدد دیتا ہے۔
examples.note: Courage and difficulty are Abstract Nouns. Courage is the singular subject and takes helps.

rules: An **Abstract Noun** names an **idea, quality, feeling, or state**.
Abstract Nouns are often **uncountable** and take a **singular verb**.
Use an Abstract Noun to discuss an **idea or quality**, not a physical object.

commonMistakes.wrong: Honest is important in public service.
commonMistakes.right: Honesty is important in public service.
commonMistakes.urdu: عوامی خدمت میں ایمانداری اہم ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Honesty is the noun naming the quality; honest is an adjective.

commonMistakes.wrong: Justice are necessary.
commonMistakes.right: Justice is necessary.
commonMistakes.urdu: انصاف ضروری ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Justice is one Abstract Noun, so it takes is.

commonMistakes.wrong: The policy gave many hopes.
commonMistakes.right: The policy gave hope.
commonMistakes.urdu: پالیسی نے امید دی۔
commonMistakes.note: Hope is normally uncountable when it means a general feeling.

practice.question: Which is an abstract noun?
practice.explanation: Honesty names a quality that cannot be touched.

practice.question: Choose the noun formed from “brave”.
practice.explanation: Bravery is the standard abstract noun.

quiz.question: Which is abstract in “Justice should be equal”?
quiz.explanation: Justice names an idea.

quiz.question: Choose the correct verb.
quiz.explanation: Knowledge is singular and uncountable.

quiz.question: Which sentence has an abstract noun?
quiz.explanation: Courage names a quality.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form.
quiz.explanation: Advice is uncountable.

quiz.question: Which names a feeling?
quiz.explanation: Happiness names a feeling.

ruleExamples: **Courage** helped the candidate face the interview.

types.name: Countable Noun
types.description: A Countable Noun can be counted and has singular and plural forms.
types.urduExplanation: قابلِ شمار اسم کو گنا جا سکتا ہے اور اس کی واحد اور جمع شکلیں ہوتی ہیں۔

examples.text: One candidate submitted a form.
examples.urdu: ایک امیدوار نے فارم جمع کرایا۔
examples.note: Candidate and form are Countable Nouns. The singular subject one candidate takes submitted in the past tense.

examples.text: Three candidates passed the test.
examples.urdu: تین امیدوار امتحان میں کامیاب ہوئے۔
examples.note: Candidates is the plural form of the Countable Noun candidate. The plural subject takes passed in the past tense.

examples.text: The examiner checked two answers.
examples.urdu: ممتحن نے دو جوابات چیک کیے۔
examples.note: Answers is a plural Countable Noun because two answers can be counted.

examples.text: Several questions appeared in the paper.
examples.urdu: پرچے میں کئی سوالات آئے۔
examples.note: Questions is a plural Countable Noun. Several is used with a plural countable noun.

rules: A singular **Countable Noun** can take **a** or **an**.
Use **numbers** such as one, two, or several with Countable Nouns.
Plural Countable Nouns can take **many**, **few**, or **several**.

commonMistakes.wrong: She bought two book.
commonMistakes.right: She bought two books.
commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے دو کتابیں خریدیں۔
commonMistakes.note: A number greater than one needs the plural form books.

commonMistakes.wrong: There is many candidates.
commonMistakes.right: There are many candidates.
commonMistakes.urdu: وہاں بہت سے امیدوار ہیں۔
commonMistakes.note: Candidates is plural, so use are.

commonMistakes.wrong: I saw an candidates.
commonMistakes.right: I saw a candidate.
commonMistakes.urdu: میں نے ایک امیدوار دیکھا۔
commonMistakes.note: A singular noun takes a before the consonant sound in candidate.

practice.question: Choose the correct plural form.
practice.explanation: Criteria is the plural of criterion in formal English.

quiz.explanation: Pens can be counted.

types.name: Uncountable Noun
types.description: An Uncountable Noun names a substance, idea, or mass that is not counted separately.
types.urduExplanation: ناقابلِ شمار اسم ایسی چیز، مادے یا خیال کا نام ہے جسے الگ الگ نہیں گنا جاتا۔

examples.text: The research is useful for the examination.
examples.urdu: تحقیق امتحان کے لیے مفید ہے۔
examples.note: Research is an Uncountable Noun, so it takes the singular verb is. It is not normally written as researches for general research.

examples.text: The information was accurate.
examples.urdu: معلومات درست تھیں۔
examples.note: Information is Uncountable and takes the singular verb was. Do not write informations.

examples.text: The equipment is new.
examples.urdu: آلات نئے ہیں۔
examples.note: Equipment is Uncountable in English and takes is. Use pieces of equipment when counting items.

examples.text: The committee needs more evidence.
examples.urdu: کمیٹی کو مزید شواہد کی ضرورت ہے۔
examples.note: Evidence is Uncountable here, so more is used without a plural s.

rules: An **Uncountable Noun** names a substance, idea, or mass that is not normally counted separately.
Uncountable Nouns normally take a **singular verb**.
Use **much**, **little**, or **some**, not **a** or **an**, with many Uncountable Nouns.

commonMistakes.wrong: The information are useful.
commonMistakes.right: The information is useful.
commonMistakes.urdu: معلومات مفید ہیں۔
commonMistakes.note: Information is Uncountable in English, so it takes is.

commonMistakes.wrong: The researcher gave me many advices.
commonMistakes.right: The researcher gave me much advice.
commonMistakes.urdu: محقق نے مجھے بہت سے مشورے دیے۔
commonMistakes.note: Advice is Uncountable; use much advice or pieces of advice.

commonMistakes.wrong: The laboratory bought new equipments.
commonMistakes.right: The laboratory bought new equipment.
commonMistakes.urdu: لیبارٹری نے نئے آلات خریدے۔
commonMistakes.note: Equipment is Uncountable and does not normally take plural s.

practice.question: Choose the correct phrase.
practice.explanation: Information is uncountable and can be used with some.

practice.question: Which sentence is correct?
practice.explanation: Furniture is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: Information takes is.

quiz.question: Which phrase is correct?
quiz.explanation: A piece of advice is countable.

quiz.question: Choose the correct determiner.
quiz.explanation: Water is uncountable.

quiz.question: Which is uncountable in “The equipment is new”?
quiz.explanation: Equipment is uncountable.

quiz.question: Choose the correct verb.
quiz.explanation: Furniture takes is.

types.name: Material Noun
types.description: A Material Noun names a substance from which things are made.
types.urduExplanation: اسمِ مادہ اس چیز یا مادے کا نام ہے جس سے دوسری چیزیں بنائی جاتی ہیں۔

examples.text: The bridge is made of steel.
examples.urdu: پل فولاد سے بنا ہوا ہے۔
examples.note: Steel is a Material Noun naming the substance. Made of shows the material used; made by would name the maker.

examples.text: The table is made of wood.
examples.urdu: میز لکڑی سے بنی ہوئی ہے۔
examples.note: Wood is a Material Noun. Made of is correct because wood remains the material of the table.

examples.text: The officer wore a gold badge.
examples.urdu: افسر نے سونے کا بیج پہنا۔
examples.note: Gold is a Material Noun naming the substance used in the badge.

examples.text: The bottle is made from recycled plastic.
examples.urdu: بوتل ری سائیکل شدہ پلاسٹک سے بنی ہے۔
examples.note: Plastic is a Material Noun. Made from is used because the original material changes during production.

rules: A **Material Noun** names a **substance or material**.
Material Nouns are usually **uncountable** when they refer to material in general.
Use **made of** when the material is still easy to recognize.

commonMistakes.wrong: The chair is made for wood.
commonMistakes.right: The chair is made of wood.
commonMistakes.urdu: کرسی لکڑی سے بنی ہوئی ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Made of names the material; made for means purpose, not material.

commonMistakes.wrong: The bridge is made by steel.
commonMistakes.right: The bridge is made of steel.
commonMistakes.urdu: پل فولاد سے بنا ہوا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Made by normally names the maker, while made of names the material.

commonMistakes.wrong: The badge is made with gold.
commonMistakes.right: The badge is made of gold.
commonMistakes.urdu: بیج سونے سے بنا ہوا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Made of is the standard expression for the material of an object.

practice.question: Which is a material noun?
practice.explanation: Copper names a material.

practice.question: Choose the correct sentence.
practice.explanation: Water is normally uncountable and takes is.

quiz.question: Which is material in “The ring is silver”?
quiz.explanation: Silver names the material.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: Gold is uncountable.

quiz.question: Which is material in “The shirt is cotton”?
quiz.explanation: Cotton names the substance.

quiz.question: Choose the correct expression.
quiz.explanation: Use a unit to count steel.

quiz.question: Which uses a material noun correctly?
options: The chair is made of wood.
A wood is on the table.
quiz.explanation: Wood is an uncountable material.

types.name: Compound Noun
types.description: A Compound Noun is made by joining two or more words to name one person, place, thing, or idea.
types.urduExplanation: مرکب اسم دو یا دو سے زیادہ الفاظ کو ملا کر ایک شخص، جگہ، چیز یا خیال کا نام بناتا ہے۔

examples.text: The examination hall opens at eight o’clock.
examples.urdu: امتحانی ہال آٹھ بجے کھلتا ہے۔
examples.note: Examination hall is a Compound Noun made from examination and hall. It names one place, so the singular verb opens is used.

examples.text: The research report is complete.
examples.urdu: تحقیقی رپورٹ مکمل ہے۔
examples.note: Research report is a Compound Noun made from research and report. It names one document.

examples.text: The policymaker announced a new plan.
examples.urdu: پالیسی ساز نے نیا منصوبہ سنایا۔
examples.note: Policymaker is a Compound Noun made from policy and maker. It names one person.

examples.text: The civil-service exam begins tomorrow.
examples.urdu: سول سروس کا امتحان کل شروع ہوتا ہے۔
examples.note: Civil-service exam is a Compound Noun phrase naming one examination.

rules: A **Compound Noun** joins **two or more words** to give one meaning.
Compound Nouns may be written as **one word, two words, or with a hyphen**.
In a compound noun, identify the **complete expression**, not only one word.

commonMistakes.wrong: The examination halls opens early.
commonMistakes.right: The examination hall opens early.
commonMistakes.urdu: امتحانی ہال جلد کھلتا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: One hall is singular, so use hall and opens.

commonMistakes.wrong: The policymaker make a plan.
commonMistakes.right: The policymaker makes a plan.
commonMistakes.urdu: پالیسی ساز منصوبہ بناتا ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: Policymaker is one singular Compound Noun, so the verb is makes.

commonMistakes.wrong: The civil service exam are difficult.
commonMistakes.right: The civil-service exam is difficult.
commonMistakes.urdu: سول سروس کا امتحان مشکل ہے۔
commonMistakes.note: One exam is singular, so use is; the compound may be written with a hyphen.

quiz.explanation: Toothbrush takes -es.

quiz.explanation: Mother receives the plural ending.

rules: A noun can work as the subject, object, complement, or object of a preposition.
Check capitalization, articles, plural forms, and verb agreement when identifying a noun in an exam sentence.
Some nouns change category according to meaning and context; do not memorize a label without reading the sentence.

examples.text: Ali is carrying a pen to school.
examples.urdu: علی ایک قلم لے کر اسکول جا رہا ہے۔
examples.note: Ali is a person, pen is a thing, and school is a place; all are Nouns.

commonMistakes.wrong: He gave me many useful advices.
commonMistakes.right: He gave me much useful advice.
commonMistakes.note: Advice is uncountable in standard English.

commonMistakes.wrong: The team are ready as one unit.
commonMistakes.right: The team is ready as one unit.
commonMistakes.note: Use a singular verb when a collective noun acts together.

commonMistakes.wrong: I visited islamabad in july.
commonMistakes.right: I visited Islamabad in July.
commonMistakes.note: Proper nouns and month names begin with capital letters.

examTips: In an error-detection question, first identify whether the noun is singular, plural, countable, or uncountable.
Remember irregular plurals and foreign plurals such as child/children, criterion/criteria, and phenomenon/phenomena.
For collective nouns, decide whether the group acts as one unit or as separate members before choosing the verb.

practice.question: Which word is a proper noun in “The delegation visited Lahore”?
practice.explanation: Lahore is the specific name of a city.

practice.question: Choose the correct sentence.
practice.explanation: Advice is uncountable and is used with some.

practice.question: Which is a material noun?
practice.explanation: Iron names a material.

quiz.question: What is the correct plural of “mother-in-law”?
quiz.explanation: The main noun mother takes the plural ending.

quiz.question: Which noun is abstract?
quiz.explanation: Freedom names an idea.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: Information is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

content.summary: Nouns name people, places, animals, things, materials, or ideas. For exam questions, identify the noun type, then check capitalization, articles, number, plural formation, possessive form, and subject–verb agreement. Context matters because one noun can have different classifications in different sentences.

content.introduction: A preposition is a word that shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence, often indicating place, time, direction, or manner. Prepositions are small words but they cause frequent errors because their usage often does not translate directly between Urdu and English. Mastering common prepositional patterns is essential for accurate writing in CSS, PMS, and IELTS exams.
content.urduExplanation: Preposition وہ لفظ ہے جو noun یا pronoun کا کسی دوسرے لفظ سے تعلق ظاہر کرتا ہے، جیسے جگہ، وقت یا سمت بتانے کے لیے 'in', 'on', 'at' جیسے الفاظ استعمال ہوتے ہیں۔ یہ ہمیشہ noun یا pronoun سے پہلے آتا ہے، جیسے 'on the table' یا 'at school'۔ چونکہ اردو اور انگریزی میں prepositions کا استعمال مختلف ہوتا ہے، اس لیے طلبہ کو اکثر ان میں غلطی لگ جاتی ہے۔ اس لیے مخصوص phrases اور idioms کے ساتھ صحیح preposition یاد کرنا بہت ضروری ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Prepositions connect nouns or pronouns to other words in a sentence, showing relationships of time, place, direction, cause, or manner. Common prepositions include in, on, at, by, with, for, from, and to, each used in specific contexts that often must simply be memorized. Prepositions are always followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund (a verb form ending in -ing), never by a bare infinitive. Many errors occur because prepositions do not translate word-for-word between languages, so it is important to learn fixed prepositional phrases like 'interested in', 'good at', and 'depend on' as whole units.

types.name: Preposition of Time
types.description: Shows when something happens, e.g., at 6 o'clock, on Monday, in July.

types.name: Preposition of Place
types.description: Shows where something is located, e.g., at the station, on the table, in the room.

types.name: Preposition of Direction
types.description: Shows movement toward or away from something, e.g., to school, into the room, out of the house.

types.name: Preposition of Manner
types.description: Shows how something is done, e.g., by bus, with care, in silence.

types.name: Preposition of Agent/Instrument
types.description: Shows who or what performs or is used for an action, e.g., written by the author, cut with a knife.

rules: Use 'at' for exact times and specific points (at 5 p.m., at the bus stop), 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on 14 August), and 'in' for longer periods and enclosed spaces (in 2026, in the room).
A preposition is always followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund, never by the base form of a verb (interested in learning, not interested in learn).
Many verbs and adjectives are fixed with specific prepositions and must be memorized, such as 'good at', 'afraid of', 'depend on', and 'listen to'.
Do not drop necessary prepositions that exist in English even if the Urdu sentence structure does not require an equivalent word.
In formal writing, avoid ending a sentence with a preposition when a more formal structure is available (To whom did you give the letter? rather than Who did you give the letter to?).
Do not confuse similar prepositions like 'in time' (before a deadline) and 'on time' (exactly at the scheduled time).

examples.text: The meeting is scheduled at 10 a.m. on Friday.
examples.note: preposition of time

examples.text: The keys are on the table near the door.
examples.note: preposition of place

examples.text: She walked into the examination hall confidently.
examples.note: preposition of direction

examples.text: He solved the problem with great patience.
examples.note: preposition of manner

examples.text: The novel was written by a famous Pakistani author.
examples.note: preposition of agent

examples.text: I am interested in learning new languages.
examples.note: fixed preposition after adjective

examples.text: Success depends on consistent hard work.
examples.note: fixed preposition after verb

commonMistakes.wrong: I am good in mathematics.
commonMistakes.right: I am good at mathematics.
commonMistakes.note: the fixed expression uses 'good at', not 'good in'

commonMistakes.wrong: She arrived to the airport late.
commonMistakes.right: She arrived at the airport late.
commonMistakes.note: 'arrive' takes 'at' for specific places, not 'to'

commonMistakes.wrong: He is married with a doctor.
commonMistakes.right: He is married to a doctor.
commonMistakes.note: the correct fixed preposition after 'married' is 'to'

commonMistakes.wrong: We discussed about the plan yesterday.
commonMistakes.right: We discussed the plan yesterday.
commonMistakes.note: 'discuss' is directly transitive in English and does not need 'about'

practice.question: Choose the correct preposition: 'The exam will be held ___ Monday.'
practice.explanation: 'On' is used with specific days of the week, such as Monday.

practice.question: Select the correct sentence.
practice.explanation: The fixed prepositional phrase is 'afraid of', not 'afraid from' or other combinations.

practice.question: Choose the correctly completed sentence: 'He is responsible ___ managing the entire project.'
practice.explanation: 'Responsible for' is the correct fixed prepositional phrase in English.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses the preposition of time correctly?
options: The event will happen in 6 p.m.
The event will happen at 6 p.m.
The event will happen on 6 p.m.
The event will happen by 6 p.m. sharp only.
quiz.explanation: 'At' is used with exact clock times such as 6 p.m.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He is capable to solve this problem.
He is capable of solving this problem.
He is capable for solving this problem.
He is capable at solving this problem.
quiz.explanation: 'Capable of' followed by a gerund is the correct fixed prepositional structure.

quiz.question: Select the sentence with the correct preposition of place.
options: She is waiting in the bus stop.
She is waiting on the bus stop.
She is waiting at the bus stop.
She is waiting to the bus stop.
quiz.explanation: 'At' is used for specific points like a bus stop.

content.summary: Prepositions show relationships of time, place, direction, or manner between words in a sentence and are always followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund. Many prepositions are fixed with specific verbs and adjectives, such as 'good at' and 'depend on', and must be memorized rather than translated directly from Urdu. Careful attention to at/on/in distinctions and fixed phrases prevents the most frequent prepositional errors.

content.introduction: A pronoun replaces a noun or noun phrase to avoid repetition. In competitive exams, check its antecedent, number, person, gender, and subject/object case.
content.urduExplanation: Pronoun وہ لفظ ہے جو noun یا noun phrase کی جگہ آتا ہے۔ امتحانات میں اس کا درست انتخاب antecedent، واحد/جمع، شخص، جنس اور subject/object case کے مطابق کیا جاتا ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Pronouns must clearly refer to an antecedent and agree with it. They must use the correct subject, object, possessive, reflexive, or relative form.

types.name: Personal Pronoun
types.description: Replaces a person or thing and changes according to person, number, and subject/object case.
types.urduExplanation: Personal pronoun کسی شخص یا چیز کی جگہ آتا ہے اور subject یا object کے مطابق بدلتا ہے۔
types.subjectVerbAgreement: The panel issues its ruling, and it notifies the candidates immediately. Subject 'the panel' is a singular collective noun, so singular verbs 'issues' and 'notifies' are used; the pronoun 'it' and possessive 'its' agree in number with 'panel', and the conjunction 'and' links two clauses with the same singular subject.

examples.referenceText: The candidates submitted the applications before the deadline.
examples.referenceUrdu: امیدواروں نے آخری تاریخ سے پہلے درخواستیں جمع کرائیں۔
examples.text: They submitted them before the deadline.
examples.urdu: انہوں نے انہیں آخری تاریخ سے پہلے جمع کرا دیا۔
examples.note: 'They' replaces 'the candidates' as a plural subject, while 'them' replaces 'the applications' as a plural object pronoun.

examples.referenceText: I reviewed the policy document before the committee asked me to present the findings.
examples.referenceUrdu: میں نے پالیسی کی دستاویز کا جائزہ لیا، اس سے پہلے کہ کمیٹی نے مجھے نتائج پیش کرنے کو کہا۔
examples.text: I reviewed it before the committee asked me to present the findings.
examples.urdu: میں نے اس کا جائزہ لیا، اس سے پہلے کہ کمیٹی نے مجھے نتائج پیش کرنے کو کہا۔
examples.note: 'I' is a first-person singular subject and 'me' is a first-person singular object; 'it' replaces the policy document.

examples.referenceText: The researcher completed the analysis, and the supervisor praised the researcher.
examples.referenceUrdu: محقق نے تجزیہ مکمل کیا اور نگران نے محقق کی تعریف کی۔
examples.text: The researcher completed the analysis, and the supervisor praised her.
examples.urdu: محقق نے تجزیہ مکمل کیا اور نگران نے اس کی تعریف کی۔
examples.note: 'Her' is a third-person singular female object pronoun referring to 'the researcher'.

examples.referenceText: We submitted the proposal to the commission, and the commission replied to us.
examples.referenceUrdu: ہم نے کمیشن کو تجویز جمع کرائی اور کمیشن نے ہمیں جواب دیا۔
examples.text: We submitted the proposal to the commission, and it replied to us.
examples.urdu: ہم نے کمیشن کو تجویز جمع کرائی اور اس نے ہمیں جواب دیا۔
examples.note: 'We' is a first-person plural subject, 'it' refers to the singular commission, and 'us' is a first-person plural object pronoun.

rules: Replaces a person or thing and changes according to person, number, and subject/object case.

commonMistakes.wrong: Him submitted the application.
commonMistakes.right: He submitted the application.
commonMistakes.urdu: اس نے درخواست جمع کروائی۔
commonMistakes.note: Him submitted the application. → He submitted the application.: 'Him' is an object pronoun incorrectly used as the subject; replace it with the subject pronoun 'he'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The officer spoke to I.
commonMistakes.right: The officer spoke to me.
commonMistakes.urdu: افسر نے مجھ سے بات کی۔
commonMistakes.note: The officer spoke to I. → The officer spoke to me.: 'I' is a subject pronoun but is the object of the preposition 'to'; the correct object pronoun is 'me'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Each of the candidates must submit their affidavit.
commonMistakes.right: Each of the candidates must submit his or her affidavit.
commonMistakes.urdu: امیدواروں میں سے ہر ایک کو اپنا حلف نامہ جمع کروانا ہوگا۔
commonMistakes.note: Each of the candidates must submit their affidavit. → Each of the candidates must submit his or her affidavit.: 'Each' is grammatically singular and requires a singular pronoun, so 'their' should be replaced by 'his or her' in formal usage.

practice.explanation: The correct form must fit the pronoun type and sentence role.

practice.question: Choose the correct verb: Each candidate ___ prepared.
practice.explanation: Each is singular, so has is required.

practice.explanation: The first sentence follows the relevant pronoun and agreement rule.

practice.question: Select the correct object pronoun: The panel invited ___.
practice.explanation: Me is an object pronoun after invited.
