content.introduction: A gerund phrase consists of a gerund (a verb ending in -ing used as a noun) together with its objects, complements, and modifiers. The entire phrase functions as a noun in the sentence — as subject, object, or complement. Gerund phrases are a frequent source of errors in CSS/PMS sentence-correction and IELTS Writing Task 2. Like all phrases, a gerund phrase contains no subject–verb pair.
content.urduExplanation: Gerund phrase میں ایک gerund (یعنی -ing form جو noun کا کام کرے) اور اس کے objects یا modifiers شامل ہوتے ہیں۔ یہ پورا گروہ جملے میں noun کی طرح کام کرتا ہے — subject، object یا complement کے طور پر۔ مثلاً 'Reading difficult books' ایک gerund phrase ہے جو جملے میں subject کا کام کر رہا ہے: 'Reading difficult books improves vocabulary.'۔ Gerund کے subject کو possessive form میں لانا ضروری ہے: 'His arriving late annoyed everyone.'۔ CSS اور PMS میں gerund اور infinitive کے درمیان فرق اور صحیح استعمال بہت اہم امتحانی نکتہ ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: A gerund phrase is a non-finite verb phrase headed by a gerund (-ing form functioning as a noun). It can be the subject of a sentence ('Swimming in cold rivers requires endurance'), a direct object ('She enjoys reading classic novels'), an indirect object, the object of a preposition ('He was praised for submitting the report on time'), or a subject complement ('Her hobby is collecting rare stamps'). The gerund itself can take objects, subject complements, adverbials, and even its own implied subject, which is expressed in the possessive case when stated explicitly: 'We appreciated him/his arriving early.' Gerunds differ from present participles in function: gerunds act as nouns, participles act as adjectives. Both look identical in form (-ing); only context and function distinguish them. Some verbs take only gerunds as objects (enjoy, avoid, deny, finish, consider, suggest, postpone), while others take only infinitives (want, hope, decide, agree, refuse). A few take both with different meanings (stop, remember, try).

types.name: Gerund Phrase as Subject
types.description: The entire phrase acts as the grammatical subject: 'Writing concise answers helps in CSS examinations.'

types.name: Gerund Phrase as Direct Object
types.description: Follows verbs that take gerund objects: 'She avoided making unnecessary comments.'

types.name: Gerund Phrase as Object of a Preposition
types.description: Follows a preposition: 'He was fined for crossing the red light.'

types.name: Gerund Phrase as Subject Complement
types.description: Follows a linking verb and describes the subject: 'His main weakness is procrastinating on important tasks.'

types.name: Gerund Phrase with Possessive Subject
types.description: When the logical subject of the gerund is expressed, it appears in the possessive case: 'The teacher disapproved of the student's cheating on the test.'

rules: A gerund phrase always begins with an -ing verb form functioning as a noun; it performs all noun roles in the sentence.
Certain verbs are always followed by a gerund, never an infinitive: enjoy, avoid, finish, deny, suggest, consider, postpone, practise, risk, mind, keep.
The implied or stated logical subject of a gerund should be in the possessive case in formal writing: 'We object to their changing the rules.'
A gerund phrase at the beginning of a sentence is treated as a singular noun for subject–verb agreement purposes.
A gerund phrase as object of a preposition must immediately follow the preposition ('interested in applying', not 'interested to apply').

Do not confuse the gerund phrase with the present participial phrase: if the -ing phrase acts as a noun, it is a gerund phrase; if it acts as an adjective or begins a modifying phrase, it is participial.

examples.text: Practising past papers regularly is the most effective preparation strategy.
examples.note: 'Practising past papers regularly' is the gerund phrase functioning as the subject. The gerund 'practising' takes the object 'past papers' and the adverb 'regularly'.

examples.text: She suggested postponing the meeting until the report was ready.
examples.note: 'Postponing the meeting until the report was ready' is the gerund phrase (direct object of 'suggested').

examples.text: He was penalised for submitting the form after the deadline.
examples.note: 'Submitting the form after the deadline' — gerund phrase as object of the preposition 'for'.

examples.text: The board's insisting on transparency improved public trust.
examples.note: 'The board's insisting on transparency' — gerund phrase with possessive subject 'the board's', functioning as the subject of the main clause.

examples.text: His greatest accomplishment was solving the long-standing water crisis.
examples.note: 'Solving the long-standing water crisis' is the gerund phrase used as subject complement.

commonMistakes.wrong: She is interested to apply for the position.
commonMistakes.right: She is interested in applying for the position.
commonMistakes.note: After prepositions, a gerund (not an infinitive) is required: 'interested in applying'.

commonMistakes.wrong: I appreciate you to help me with the project.
commonMistakes.right: I appreciate your helping me with the project.
commonMistakes.note: 'Appreciate' takes a gerund object; the logical subject of the gerund must be in the possessive case in formal writing.

commonMistakes.wrong: Swim in the sea are dangerous.
commonMistakes.right: Swimming in the sea is dangerous.
commonMistakes.note: A gerund phrase subject requires the -ing form and takes a singular verb.

commonMistakes.wrong: He avoided to make mistakes.
commonMistakes.right: He avoided making mistakes.
commonMistakes.note: 'Avoid' is a verb that takes a gerund object, never an infinitive.

practice.question: Identify the gerund phrase in: 'The government considered implementing stricter environmental regulations.'
practice.explanation: 'Implementing stricter environmental regulations' is the gerund phrase (direct object of 'considered'). 'Implementing' is the gerund head, taking 'stricter environmental regulations' as its object.

practice.question: Which verb CANNOT be followed by a gerund?
practice.explanation: 'Want' takes an infinitive object: 'I want to go', never 'I want going'. The other three (avoid, suggest, finish) take gerund objects.

practice.question: Choose the correct sentence using a gerund phrase as a subject.
options: To read widely are important for CSS.
Reading widely are important for CSS.
Reading widely is important for CSS.
Read widely is important for CSS.
practice.explanation: A gerund phrase subject ('Reading widely') takes a singular verb ('is'). 'To read widely' is an infinitive phrase; a bare infinitive 'Read' cannot be a subject.

quiz.question: In 'The teacher disapproved of the student's copying during the test', 'the student's copying during the test' is:
options: A gerund phrase acting as object of the preposition 'of'
quiz.explanation: 'The student's copying during the test' is a gerund phrase (gerund 'copying' + adverbial 'during the test') with possessive subject 'student's', serving as the object of the preposition 'of'.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses a gerund phrase?
options: She enjoys to read historical novels.
He finished to write the essay.
They suggested to postpone the vote.
Maintaining accurate records is essential for good governance.
quiz.explanation: 'Maintaining accurate records' is a correctly formed gerund phrase as subject, with singular verb 'is'. 'Enjoy', 'finish', and 'suggest' all require gerund (not infinitive) objects.

quiz.question: Identify the difference: 'Running is good exercise' vs. 'The man running the race is my brother.' What are 'running' in each?
options: First is a gerund (noun); second is a present participle (adjective).
First is a present participle; second is a gerund.
quiz.explanation: In 'Running is good exercise', 'running' is a gerund (subject noun). In 'the man running the race', 'running the race' is a participial phrase modifying 'man' adjectivally.

content.summary: A gerund phrase is headed by an -ing verb form acting as a noun, and includes its objects, complements, and modifiers. It can serve as subject, direct object, object of a preposition, or subject complement. Certain verbs (enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest) always take gerund objects; the logical subject of a gerund is expressed in the possessive case. The gerund phrase contains no subject–verb pair and is distinguished from a participial phrase by its noun function.

content.introduction: An infinitive phrase consists of 'to' + the base form of a verb, along with any objects, complements, or modifiers. It is highly versatile: it can function as a noun (subject or object), an adjective (modifying a noun), or an adverb (modifying a verb, adjective, or clause). Infinitive phrases appear throughout CSS/PMS grammar tasks and IELTS writing, and are a key topic in verb-complementation questions. They have no subject–verb pair and are therefore phrases, not clauses.
content.urduExplanation: Infinitive phrase 'to' اور base verb کا مجموعہ ہے، جس میں objects اور modifiers بھی شامل ہو سکتے ہیں۔ یہ تین طرح کام کر سکتا ہے: noun (subject یا object)، adjective (noun کو modify کرے) اور adverb (verb یا adjective کو modify کرے)۔ مثلاً 'To serve the nation' noun function میں subject ہے؛ 'a chance to succeed' میں adjective function ہے؛ 'She studied to pass the exam' میں adverb function ہے۔ Infinitive phrase میں اپنا subject اور verb نہیں ہوتا — یہی اسے clause سے الگ کرتا ہے۔ CSS/PMS میں split infinitive اور bare infinitive کے صحیح استعمال سے متعلق سوالات اکثر آتے ہیں۔
content.englishExplanation: An infinitive phrase is a non-finite construction built on 'to + base verb' (the to-infinitive). It can contain a direct object, a subject complement, adverbials, and even its own logical subject introduced by 'for': 'It is important for candidates to read the instructions carefully.' As a noun: 'To lead effectively requires vision' (subject); 'She hopes to secure a promotion' (object). As an adjective: 'She had several documents to review' (post-modifying 'documents'). As an adverb: 'He trained hard to qualify for the final stage' (purpose); 'She was relieved to hear the news' (cause/reason). The bare infinitive (without 'to') follows modal verbs and certain verbs (make, let, have, see, hear, feel, watch, help). A split infinitive places an adverb between 'to' and the base verb: 'to boldly go'; while not ungrammatical, it is avoided in formal writing. Do not confuse the infinitive phrase with a prepositional phrase: 'to the market' has a noun object (prepositional phrase); 'to buy groceries' has a verb (infinitive phrase).

types.name: Infinitive Phrase Functioning as Noun (Subject)
types.description: The phrase acts as the grammatical subject: 'To speak clearly is a vital skill for a civil servant.'

types.name: Infinitive Phrase Functioning as Noun (Object)
types.description: The phrase acts as the direct object of the main verb: 'She decided to contest the election.'

types.name: Infinitive Phrase Functioning as Adjective
types.description: Post-modifies a noun or pronoun: 'The last candidate to arrive missed the briefing.'

types.name: Infinitive Phrase Functioning as Adverb (Purpose)
types.description: Expresses the purpose of the action: 'He studied relentlessly to pass the CSS examination.'

types.name: Infinitive Phrase Functioning as Adverb (Cause/Result/Condition)
types.description: Expresses cause, result, or condition: 'She was fortunate to receive a scholarship'; 'The task proved too difficult to complete.'

types.name: Infinitive Phrase with Explicit Subject (for + noun/pronoun + to-infinitive)
types.description: The logical subject is introduced by 'for': 'It is essential for every candidate to understand the syllabus.'

rules: The infinitive phrase always begins with 'to' + base verb (uninflected); it cannot be changed to match tense (*'to walked', *'to runs').
Modal verbs (can, could, will, would, may, might, shall, should, must) and certain catenative verbs (make, let, have, see, hear, feel) are followed by the bare infinitive (without 'to').
When an infinitive phrase is the subject, the sentence often uses a 'dummy it' subject and moves the infinitive to the end: 'It is impossible to overstate the importance of this rule.'
The logical subject of an infinitive phrase introduced by 'for' must be in the objective case: 'for them to decide', not 'for they to decide'.
Avoid splitting infinitives in formal/exam writing: write 'to examine carefully' rather than 'to carefully examine'.

The perfect infinitive ('to have done') indicates an action that was completed before the time of the main verb or a hypothetical past: 'She appears to have passed.'; 'He ought to have submitted the form.'

examples.text: To master English grammar thoroughly requires consistent daily practice.
examples.note: 'To master English grammar thoroughly' is the infinitive phrase acting as subject; 'grammar' is its object, 'thoroughly' is its adverb.

examples.text: The government plans to introduce a new policy on digital infrastructure.
examples.note: 'To introduce a new policy on digital infrastructure' is the infinitive phrase (direct object of 'plans').

examples.text: She was the first female officer to command the division.
examples.note: 'To command the division' is an infinitive phrase functioning as an adjective, post-modifying 'officer'.

examples.text: He worked overtime to meet the project deadline.
examples.note: 'To meet the project deadline' is an infinitive phrase of purpose, modifying the verb 'worked' adverbially.

examples.text: It is crucial for all FPSC aspirants to review past papers carefully.
examples.note: 'For all FPSC aspirants to review past papers carefully' — infinitive phrase with explicit logical subject introduced by 'for'.

commonMistakes.wrong: She made him to apologise to the committee.
commonMistakes.right: She made him apologise to the committee.
commonMistakes.note: After causative 'make', the bare infinitive (without 'to') is required.

commonMistakes.wrong: He ought to submitted the form before the deadline.
commonMistakes.right: He ought to have submitted the form before the deadline.
commonMistakes.note: When the infinitive refers to a past unfulfilled obligation, use the perfect infinitive 'to have + past participle'.

commonMistakes.wrong: To running in the park is her hobby.
commonMistakes.right: Running in the park is her hobby.
commonMistakes.note: 'To running' is not a valid infinitive form. For a noun function, either use the plain infinitive 'To run...' or the gerund 'Running...'. The gerund is more natural as subject here.

commonMistakes.wrong: I want for you to come to the ceremony.
commonMistakes.right: I want you to come to the ceremony.
commonMistakes.note: After 'want', the infinitive phrase with explicit subject does not use 'for': it is 'want + object + to-infinitive'.

practice.question: In 'The judge was the last person to deliver a verdict', what is the function of 'to deliver a verdict'?
practice.explanation: 'To deliver a verdict' post-modifies the noun 'person', answering 'which person?' — adjectival infinitive phrase.

practice.question: Which sentence correctly uses the perfect infinitive?
options: She seems to be working hard before the exam.
He appears to have submitted the form yesterday.
They claim to work on the project last year.
We need to have arriving early.
practice.explanation: 'To have submitted' is the perfect infinitive, correctly indicating that the submission occurred before the present moment. 'To be working' is progressive; 'to work' in option C is not past enough; option D is ungrammatical.

practice.question: Which verb takes the BARE infinitive (without 'to')?
practice.explanation: 'Let' is a causative verb that takes the bare infinitive: 'Let him speak.' 'Decide', 'hope', and 'plan' take the to-infinitive.

quiz.question: In 'It is necessary for every civil servant to file the annual declaration', 'for every civil servant to file the annual declaration' is:
options: An infinitive phrase with an explicit logical subject
quiz.explanation: The construction 'for + noun phrase + to-infinitive' is an infinitive phrase with an explicit logical subject. 'Every civil servant' is the logical subject of 'to file'.

quiz.question: Identify the sentence in which the infinitive phrase functions as an adverb of purpose.
options: He has the ability to analyse complex issues.
She studied intensively to clear the CSS written exam.
His plan is to restructure the department.
quiz.explanation: 'To clear the CSS written exam' answers 'why did she study?' — purpose. Option A is noun (subject); B is adjectival; D is noun (subject complement).

quiz.question: Which sentence contains an error in infinitive usage?
options: She let the candidate answer the question.
He helped them to complete the project.
They made him to sign the document.
I saw her leave the building.
quiz.explanation: 'Made him to sign' is incorrect. After causative 'make', the bare infinitive is required: 'made him sign'. 'Let', 'see', and 'help' may take bare or to-infinitive.

content.summary: An infinitive phrase consists of 'to + base verb' together with its objects, complements, and modifiers. It functions as a noun (subject/object), adjective (post-modifier of a noun), or adverb (expressing purpose, cause, or result). Modal and certain causative verbs require the bare infinitive; the perfect infinitive ('to have + past participle') signals a completed or hypothetical past action. Split infinitives are avoided in formal writing, and infinitive phrases contain no subject–verb pair.

content.introduction: A noun phrase is a group of words built around a noun or pronoun that together act as a single noun in a sentence. It can function as the subject, object, complement, or appositive of a clause. Recognising noun phrases is essential for CSS/PMS sentence-correction tasks and IELTS reading comprehension. Unlike a clause, a noun phrase has no subject–verb pair of its own.
content.urduExplanation: Noun phrase الفاظ کا وہ گروہ ہے جس کے مرکز میں ایک noun یا pronoun ہو اور باقی الفاظ اسے modify کریں۔ یہ پورا گروہ جملے میں subject، object یا complement کا کام کرتا ہے۔ مثال کے طور پر 'the hardworking student from Lahore' ایک noun phrase ہے جہاں 'student' head noun ہے۔ یاد رہے کہ noun phrase میں اپنا subject اور verb نہیں ہوتا، ورنہ وہ clause بن جائے گا۔ CSS اور IELTS کے امتحانات میں noun phrases کی پہچان sentence structure سمجھنے کے لیے بہت ضروری ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: A noun phrase (NP) consists of a head noun and all the words that modify or determine it — determiners (the, a, this), adjectives, participial phrases, prepositional phrases, and even relative clauses. The head word is always a noun or pronoun; every other element exists to restrict or describe it. Noun phrases perform the same grammatical roles as a single noun: subject ('The tall old man sat down'), direct object ('She read the lengthy government report'), indirect object, or subject complement. They have no internal subject–verb pair, which distinguishes them from noun clauses (e.g. 'what he said'). Pre-modifiers come before the head (articles, adjectives, nouns used as adjectives), while post-modifiers follow it (prepositional phrases, relative clauses, participial phrases). In IELTS and competitive exams, noun phrases create information density and must be parsed accurately.

types.name: Simple Noun Phrase
types.description: Contains only a determiner and a head noun, e.g. 'a book', 'the government'. Minimal but complete.

types.name: Extended Noun Phrase (Pre-modified)
types.description: One or more adjectives or other nouns placed before the head, e.g. 'the new five-year economic plan'.

types.name: Extended Noun Phrase (Post-modified)
types.description: The head noun is followed by a prepositional phrase, participial phrase, or relative clause, e.g. 'the report published last year'.

types.name: Pronoun as Noun Phrase
types.description: A single pronoun (he, she, they, it) stands alone as a complete noun phrase with no additional modifiers.

types.name: Appositive Noun Phrase
types.description: A noun phrase placed beside another to rename or describe it, e.g. 'Dr. Khan, the chief examiner, announced the results'.

rules: A noun phrase must have a head noun or pronoun; all other elements are modifiers that depend on this head.
Pre-modifiers appear in a fixed order before the head: determiner → opinion adjective → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → noun modifier → head.
Post-modifiers (prepositional phrases, participial phrases, relative clauses) follow the head noun in the order they appear.
A noun phrase, however long, has no subject–verb pair; if it contains one, it becomes a clause.
Noun phrases can be nested: the head of one NP may itself be modified by another NP ('a [basket of [fresh garden vegetables]]').
When a noun phrase is the subject of a sentence, the main verb must agree with the head noun, not with any modifier.

examples.text: The extremely dedicated civil servant from Islamabad received the award.
examples.note: 'The extremely dedicated civil servant from Islamabad' is the noun phrase functioning as subject; head noun = 'servant'.

examples.text: She submitted a lengthy, well-researched essay on economic policy.
examples.note: 'a lengthy, well-researched essay on economic policy' is the noun phrase (direct object); head = 'essay'.

examples.text: Dr. Ayesha, the principal of the college, addressed the students.
examples.note: 'the principal of the college' is an appositive noun phrase renaming 'Dr. Ayesha'.

examples.text: All the candidates who passed the written test were called for interview.
examples.note: 'All the candidates who passed the written test' — the relative clause 'who passed the written test' post-modifies the head 'candidates'.

examples.text: Reading good literature broadens the mind.
examples.note: Here 'Reading good literature' is a gerund phrase acting as a noun phrase (subject).

commonMistakes.wrong: The informations provided by the committee were incorrect.
commonMistakes.right: The information provided by the committee was incorrect.
commonMistakes.note: 'Information' is uncountable; the head noun governs subject–verb agreement, not the post-modifier.

commonMistakes.wrong: She is a very beauty girl.
commonMistakes.right: She is a very beautiful girl.
commonMistakes.note: Adjectives, not nouns, modify the head noun inside a noun phrase.

commonMistakes.wrong: He bought a leather brown old belt.
commonMistakes.right: He bought an old brown leather belt.
commonMistakes.note: Pre-modifiers must follow the fixed order: opinion → age → colour → material.

commonMistakes.wrong: The team of players are ready.
commonMistakes.right: The team of players is ready.
commonMistakes.note: Subject–verb agreement is determined by the head noun 'team', not the post-modifier 'players'.

practice.question: Identify the noun phrase functioning as the subject in: 'The newly appointed district commissioner addressed the crowd.'
practice.explanation: 'The newly appointed district commissioner' is the noun phrase; it contains the head noun 'commissioner' with pre-modifiers and functions as the subject.

practice.question: Which sentence uses the correct adjective order within a noun phrase?
options: She wore a red beautiful large dress.
She wore a beautiful large red dress.
She wore a large beautiful red dress.
She wore a red large beautiful dress.
practice.explanation: The correct pre-modifier order is opinion (beautiful) → size (large) → colour (red) → head noun (dress).

practice.question: In 'The report of the committee was tabled in parliament', which is the head noun of the subject noun phrase?
practice.explanation: 'Report' is the head noun; 'of the committee' is a post-modifying prepositional phrase. Subject–verb agreement ('was') is with 'report'.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a noun phrase?
quiz.explanation: 'Because she arrived late' is a subordinate adverbial clause (it has a subject 'she' and verb 'arrived'), not a noun phrase.

quiz.question: In 'He gave the poor farmer a bag of wheat', 'the poor farmer' is a noun phrase functioning as:
quiz.explanation: 'The poor farmer' is the indirect object (recipient of the giving); 'a bag of wheat' is the direct object.

quiz.question: Which sentence demonstrates correct subject–verb agreement when a post-modified noun phrase is the subject?
options: The quality of the essays were poor.
The quality of the essays was poor.
The quality of the essays are poor.
The quality of the essays have been poor.
quiz.explanation: The head noun of the subject NP is 'quality' (singular), so the verb must be singular: 'was'.

content.summary: A noun phrase is a noun or pronoun together with all its pre- and post-modifiers, functioning as a single noun unit in a sentence. Its head noun determines grammatical agreement; the phrase itself has no internal subject–verb pair. Pre-modifiers follow a strict order (determiner → opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → noun), while post-modifiers (prepositional phrases, relative clauses) follow the head.

content.introduction: A participial phrase is a non-finite verb phrase headed by a present participle (-ing) or past participle (-ed/-en) that functions as an adjective, modifying a noun or pronoun. It adds descriptive information efficiently and is a mark of sophisticated writing. Dangling and misplaced participial phrases are among the most tested error types in CSS/PMS and IELTS grammar correction tasks. A participial phrase contains no subject–verb pair, which is why misattribution of its implied subject is such a common error.
content.urduExplanation: Participial phrase ایک non-finite phrase ہے جس کا head present participle (-ing) یا past participle (-ed/-en) ہو اور یہ کسی noun یا pronoun کو adjective کی طرح modify کرے۔ یہ sentence کو مختصر اور معنی خیز بناتا ہے۔ مثلاً 'Walking along the river, she noticed the pollution' میں 'Walking along the river' subject 'she' کو modify کر رہا ہے۔ سب سے بڑی غلطی 'dangling participle' ہے — جب participial phrase کا منطقی subject اصل sentence میں موجود نہ ہو۔ CSS اور PMS کے Error Detection سوالات میں dangling اور misplaced participial phrases کثرت سے آتے ہیں۔
content.englishExplanation: A participial phrase (PP) is headed by a present participle (verb + -ing; e.g. 'running', 'having completed') or a past participle (e.g. 'written', 'defeated'). It functions exclusively as an adjective, modifying the nearest noun or pronoun. When placed at the beginning of a sentence, it must logically modify the grammatical subject of the main clause. Present participial phrases indicate an action simultaneous with or immediately preceding the main verb's action. Past participial phrases typically indicate a passive or completed quality of the modified noun. Perfect participial phrases ('Having reviewed the evidence') stress that the participial action was completed before the main verb's action. A dangling participle occurs when the implied subject of the participial phrase does not match the grammatical subject of the main clause — a major formal error. A misplaced participle occurs when the phrase is positioned too far from the noun it modifies, creating ambiguity or absurdity. Participial phrases have no internal subject–verb pair, which is the structural reason for dangling-modifier errors.

types.name: Present Participial Phrase
types.description: Headed by -ing form; indicates an action ongoing or simultaneous with the main verb: 'Carrying several files, she entered the office.'

types.name: Past Participial Phrase
types.description: Headed by past participle (-ed/-en); usually passive or adjectival: 'Exhausted by the long journey, the diplomat cancelled the meeting.'

types.name: Perfect Participial Phrase
types.description: Headed by 'having + past participle'; indicates completion before the main clause action: 'Having submitted the report, he left the office.'

types.name: Passive Perfect Participial Phrase
types.description: Headed by 'having been + past participle': 'Having been informed of the decision, the committee members dispersed.'

types.name: Absolute Phrase (Nominative Absolute)
types.description: A special participial construction with its own subject: 'Weather permitting, the ceremony will be held outdoors.' This is not a dangling participle because it has its own stated subject.

rules: A participial phrase must be placed as close as possible to the noun it modifies, normally immediately before or after it.
When a participial phrase opens a sentence, its implied subject must be the grammatical subject of the main clause — any mismatch creates a dangling participle.
Present participial phrases indicate an action concurrent with or just preceding the main verb; past participial phrases indicate a completed or passive quality.
Perfect participial phrases ('Having + past participle') signal that the participial action was fully completed before the main clause action began.
A participial phrase must not be confused with a gerund phrase: if the -ing phrase modifies a noun (adjective function), it is participial; if it acts as a noun, it is a gerund.
Absolute phrases (subject + participle) are not dangling because they have their own stated subject and modify the entire clause, not just the subject.

examples.text: Inspired by the speech, the volunteers worked with renewed energy.
examples.note: 'Inspired by the speech' is a past participial phrase modifying 'volunteers' (the grammatical subject). The phrase is correctly placed.

examples.text: Having secured the highest marks, she was offered a scholarship.
examples.note: 'Having secured the highest marks' — perfect participial phrase; the action of securing marks was completed before the scholarship was offered.

examples.text: The report submitted by the commission revealed serious irregularities.
examples.note: 'Submitted by the commission' — past participial phrase post-modifying 'report'. It functions adjectivally: which report?

examples.text: Walking through the old city, he noticed the blend of ancient and modern architecture.
examples.note: 'Walking through the old city' — present participial phrase modifying the subject 'he'. The subject of the main clause correctly matches the implied subject of the phrase.

examples.text: The officer, thoroughly exhausted by the lengthy proceedings, requested a recess.
examples.note: 'Thoroughly exhausted by the lengthy proceedings' — past participial phrase embedded mid-sentence as a post-modifier of 'officer'. The adverb 'thoroughly' modifies the participle 'exhausted'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Walking down the street, the rain began to fall.
commonMistakes.right: Walking down the street, she noticed that the rain had begun to fall.
commonMistakes.note: DANGLING PARTICIPLE: 'Walking down the street' implies a human subject, but the main clause's subject is 'the rain', which cannot walk. Rewrite to align the subjects.

commonMistakes.wrong: Exhausted from the journey, the bed looked very inviting.
commonMistakes.right: Exhausted from the journey, she found the bed very inviting.
commonMistakes.note: DANGLING PARTICIPLE: 'Exhausted' implies a person as subject, but the main clause's subject is 'the bed'. Correct by making the person the grammatical subject.

commonMistakes.wrong: Having been reviewed, the committee accepted the proposal.
commonMistakes.right: Having reviewed the proposal, the committee accepted it.
commonMistakes.note: If the committee did the reviewing, the phrase should be active: 'Having reviewed'. 'Having been reviewed' implies the committee was reviewed, not the proposal.

commonMistakes.wrong: She submitted a report written hurried.
commonMistakes.right: She submitted a hurriedly written report.
commonMistakes.note: Adverbs, not adjectives, modify participles. 'Hurried' is an adjective; 'hurriedly' is the correct adverb form to modify the participle 'written'.

practice.question: Identify the dangling participial phrase in the following sentences:
options: Determined to succeed, she prepared rigorously for the exam.
Having read the brief, the minister gave a detailed response.
Driving through Lahore, the Badshahi Mosque came into view.
Exhausted by the heat, the officers requested shade.
practice.explanation: 'Driving through Lahore' implies a human driver, but the main clause's subject is 'the Badshahi Mosque', which cannot drive. This is a classic dangling participle. The other three correctly align the participial phrase with a human subject.

practice.question: What is the function of the participial phrase in: 'The documents signed by the minister were sent to Islamabad'?
options: It acts as the subject of the sentence.
It acts as an adjective modifying 'documents'.
It acts as an adverb modifying 'sent'.
It acts as the main verb of the sentence.
practice.explanation: 'Signed by the minister' is a past participial phrase post-modifying the noun 'documents' (which documents? — those signed by the minister). It functions adjectivally.

practice.question: Which sentence uses a perfect participial phrase correctly?
options: Having been submitting the form, she felt relieved.
Having submitted the form, she felt relieved.
Having submit the form, she felt relieved.
Have submitted the form, she felt relieved.
practice.explanation: The perfect participial phrase is formed with 'having + past participle': 'Having submitted'. This correctly indicates that submitting was completed before feeling relieved.

quiz.question: In 'Weather permitting, the convocation will be held in the open ground', what type of construction is 'Weather permitting'?
options: A present participial phrase modifying the subject
An absolute phrase with its own stated subject
quiz.explanation: 'Weather permitting' is an absolute phrase — it has its own stated subject ('Weather') and its own participle ('permitting'). It modifies the entire main clause and is not a dangling participle.

quiz.question: Which correctly distinguishes a participial phrase from a gerund phrase?
options: A participial phrase uses -ing; a gerund phrase uses -ed.
A participial phrase functions as a noun; a gerund phrase functions as an adjective.
A participial phrase functions as an adjective; a gerund phrase functions as a noun.
They are identical in function and differ only in position.
quiz.explanation: A participial phrase always modifies a noun (adjective function). A gerund phrase always acts as a noun (subject, object, complement). Both can begin with an -ing word.

quiz.question: Correct the dangling participle: 'Having lost the key, the door could not be opened.'
options: Having lost the key, nobody could open the door.
Having lost the key, the door was locked by nobody.
The door could not be opened having lost the key.
Having been losing the key, the door refused to open.
quiz.explanation: The phrase 'Having lost the key' implies a person as subject. The corrected sentence makes 'nobody' (a person) the grammatical subject: 'Having lost the key, nobody could open the door.'

content.summary: A participial phrase is headed by a present or past participle and functions exclusively as an adjective modifying a noun or pronoun. It must be placed immediately adjacent to the noun it modifies; when fronted, its implied subject must match the main clause's grammatical subject. Dangling participles (mismatched implied subject) and misplaced participles (wrong position) are major CSS/PMS error types. Absolute phrases have their own stated subject and are not dangling. A participial phrase has no subject–verb pair.

content.introduction: A prepositional phrase consists of a preposition followed by its object (a noun phrase, pronoun, gerund, or noun clause) and any modifiers of that object. Prepositional phrases are among the most frequent phrase types in English and function either adjectivally (modifying nouns) or adverbially (modifying verbs/clauses). They are heavily tested in CSS/PMS, IELTS, and all competitive exam grammar sections. A prepositional phrase has no subject–verb pair and thus is not a clause.
content.urduExplanation: Prepositional phrase میں ایک preposition اور اس کے بعد کا object (noun phrase یا pronoun) شامل ہوتا ہے۔ یہ phrase دو طرح کام کرتا ہے: noun کو modify کرے تو adjectival اور verb کو modify کرے تو adverbial۔ مثلاً 'in the morning' adverbial prepositional phrase ہے (وقت بتا رہا ہے) اور 'the book on the table' میں 'on the table' adjectival ہے (کون سی کتاب؟)۔ اس میں اپنا subject اور verb نہیں ہوتا۔ CSS کے Grammar اور Comprehension کے سوالات میں prepositional phrases بہت زیادہ آتے ہیں۔
content.englishExplanation: A prepositional phrase (PP) is formed by a preposition (in, on, at, by, for, with, through, under, between, etc.) followed by a noun phrase as its object. The object is called the object of the preposition. Prepositional phrases function adjectivally when they post-modify a noun: 'the officer in charge', 'a student from Lahore'. They function adverbially when they modify a verb, adjective, or clause: 'She arrived at noon', 'He is good at mathematics'. Complex prepositions combine two or three words: 'because of', 'in spite of', 'on behalf of', 'according to', 'in front of'. The object of a preposition must be in the objective case (pronoun): 'between you and me', NOT 'between you and I'. Prepositional phrases may be stacked or embedded: 'the man at the top of the ladder in the corner of the room'. They do not contain a subject–verb pair; 'after she left' is an adverbial clause, while 'after the meeting' is a prepositional phrase.

types.name: Adjectival Prepositional Phrase
types.description: Post-modifies a noun or pronoun: 'the policy on taxation', 'something of great value'. Answers 'which one?' or 'what kind?'.

types.name: Adverbial Prepositional Phrase (Manner)
types.description: Modifies a verb showing how: 'He spoke with great confidence', 'She acted in a professional manner'.

types.name: Adverbial Prepositional Phrase (Time)
types.description: Indicates when or duration: 'at dawn', 'during the examination', 'for three years', 'since independence'.

types.name: Adverbial Prepositional Phrase (Place)
types.description: Indicates where: 'in Islamabad', 'at the Ministry of Finance', 'behind the court building'.

types.name: Prepositional Phrase as Subject Complement
types.description: Follows a linking verb and describes the subject: 'The book is on the shelf', 'She is in charge of the project'.

types.name: Complex Preposition Phrase
types.description: Uses multi-word prepositions: 'in accordance with the rules', 'on behalf of the government', 'in spite of the obstacles'.

rules: A prepositional phrase always begins with a preposition and must have a noun phrase (or pronoun/gerund) as its object; a preposition cannot stand alone.
The object of a preposition must be in the objective (accusative) case: 'for him/her/them/me', never 'for he/she/they/I'.
When a prepositional phrase functions adjectivally, it must immediately follow the noun it modifies to avoid ambiguity.
Prepositional phrases used adverbially can be fronted for emphasis and should then be followed by a comma: 'In times of crisis, leadership matters.'
Do not end a sentence with a preposition in formal writing when a more natural construction is available; however, in speech and informal writing it is widely accepted.
Stacked prepositional phrases can create ambiguity; restructuring is preferred for clarity in formal register.

examples.text: The minister of finance presented the budget in the National Assembly.
examples.note: 'of finance' (adjectival, modifying 'minister') and 'in the National Assembly' (adverbial of place).

examples.text: She was appointed on behalf of the provincial government.
examples.note: 'on behalf of the provincial government' is a complex prepositional phrase functioning adverbially.

examples.text: In spite of numerous obstacles, the project was completed on schedule.
examples.note: 'In spite of numerous obstacles' (adverbial of concession) is fronted and followed by a comma.

examples.text: The report on the economic crisis was submitted to the committee.
examples.note: 'on the economic crisis' — adjectival PP modifying 'report'; 'to the committee' — adverbial PP of direction.

examples.text: Between you and me, the decision was poorly made.
examples.note: Correct use of objective pronouns 'you' and 'me' as objects of the preposition 'between'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Between you and I, this is a mistake.
commonMistakes.right: Between you and me, this is a mistake.
commonMistakes.note: The object of a preposition must be in the objective case: 'me', not 'I'.

commonMistakes.wrong: She is interested for classical music.
commonMistakes.right: She is interested in classical music.
commonMistakes.note: Adjectives take fixed prepositions. 'Interested' collocates with 'in', not 'for'.

commonMistakes.wrong: I will meet you on Monday morning at 9 AM in morning.
commonMistakes.right: I will meet you on Monday morning at 9 AM.
commonMistakes.note: Redundant prepositional phrases: 'in morning' is incorrect and duplicates 'Monday morning'. Use 'in the morning' only when the day is unspecified.

commonMistakes.wrong: The student which I told you sits at the back.
commonMistakes.right: The student whom I told you about sits at the back.
commonMistakes.note: 'About' completes the prepositional phrase; stranding is acceptable in speech, but 'which' must not refer to a person.

practice.question: In 'The officials from the northern districts attended the conference in Islamabad', which prepositional phrase is adjectival?
practice.explanation: 'From the northern districts' post-modifies the noun 'officials' (which officials? — those from the northern districts), making it adjectival.

practice.question: Which sentence contains an error in the use of a prepositional phrase?
options: The decision was made in accordance with the law.
She is capable of handling complex cases.
He distributed the prizes between the three winners.
She is married with a doctor.
practice.explanation: The fixed collocation is 'married to', not 'married with'. Prepositional collocations are frequently tested in CSS/PMS.

practice.question: Which option correctly uses the objective case after a preposition?
options: This is a matter between he and the director.
The agreement is between she and the board.
The credit goes to her and the team.
Give the award to they who worked hardest.
practice.explanation: 'To her' correctly uses the objective pronoun as object of the preposition 'to'. 'He', 'she', and 'they' are subjective and incorrect after prepositions.

quiz.question: In 'A student of great determination will succeed in any exam', identify the adjectival prepositional phrase.
quiz.explanation: 'Of great determination' post-modifies the noun 'student' (what kind of student?), making it an adjectival prepositional phrase.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a complex preposition?
quiz.explanation: 'According to' is a complex (multi-word) preposition consisting of two words. The others are simple one-word prepositions.

quiz.question: Identify the sentence where the prepositional phrase is incorrectly placed (causing ambiguity).
options: She submitted the report on government corruption to the committee.
He noticed the man with a telescope in the park.
In the morning, the candidates arrived at the exam center.
The minister addressed the crowd from the stage.
quiz.explanation: 'With a telescope' is ambiguously placed — it could modify 'man' (he had a telescope) or 'noticed' (he used a telescope). It should be repositioned: 'Using a telescope, he noticed the man in the park.'

content.summary: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition followed by a noun phrase object; it functions adjectivally (modifying nouns) or adverbially (modifying verbs, adjectives, or clauses), and sometimes as a subject complement. Objects of prepositions must be in the objective case. Complex prepositions (in spite of, on behalf of, according to) are common in formal register and frequently tested in CSS/PMS. Prepositional phrases have no subject–verb pair, distinguishing them from adverbial clauses.

content.introduction: A verb phrase is the complete verb element of a clause, consisting of a main verb and any auxiliary or modal verbs that accompany it. It expresses tense, aspect, voice, and modality — the core of what a clause predicates. For CSS/PMS grammar sections and IELTS writing, mastering verb phrases is crucial for accurate tense usage and error identification. A verb phrase does not include a subject; it is strictly the verbal part of the predicate.
content.urduExplanation: Verb phrase کسی clause کا وہ حصہ ہے جس میں main verb اور اس کے ساتھ آنے والے auxiliaries یا modals شامل ہوتے ہیں۔ مثال کے طور پر 'has been working' ایک verb phrase ہے جس میں 'has been' auxiliary اور 'working' main verb ہے۔ یہ tense، aspect اور voice ظاہر کرتا ہے — یعنی بتاتا ہے کہ کام کب، کیسے اور کس نے کیا۔ یاد رہے کہ verb phrase میں subject نہیں ہوتا؛ subject باہر noun phrase میں ہوتا ہے۔ CSS کے Error Detection اور IELTS Writing میں verb phrases کی غلطیاں بہت عام ہیں، اس لیے ان کی پہچان ضروری ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: A verb phrase (VP) consists of a head main verb preceded by one or more auxiliary verbs (be, have, do) and/or modal verbs (will, would, can, could, may, might, shall, should, must, ought to). The structure follows a fixed order: (modal) + (have + past participle) + (be + present participle/past participle) + main verb. Verb phrases encode four grammatical categories: tense (past/present), aspect (simple/progressive/perfect/perfect-progressive), voice (active/passive), and modality (possibility, permission, obligation). Example: 'must have been being questioned' — modal + perfect aspect + progressive passive (rare but grammatically valid). A verb phrase is distinct from a verbal phrase (gerund, infinitive, participial phrases) in that it IS the finite verb of a clause, not a non-finite construction. In error-detection questions, candidates must identify the correct auxiliary sequence, tense consistency, and subject–verb agreement.

types.name: Simple Verb Phrase
types.description: Contains only the main verb in present or past tense, e.g. 'writes', 'arrived'. No auxiliaries.

types.name: Auxiliary + Main Verb
types.description: One auxiliary precedes the main verb: 'is writing', 'has written', 'did arrive'. Expresses aspect or emphasis.

types.name: Modal Verb Phrase
types.description: A modal precedes the main verb or an auxiliary: 'can speak', 'should have submitted', 'might be waiting'.

types.name: Passive Verb Phrase
types.description: Formed with be + past participle: 'was appointed', 'has been approved', 'will be announced'.

types.name: Perfect Progressive Verb Phrase
types.description: Combines perfect and progressive aspects: 'has been working', 'had been studying'. Shows ongoing action up to a reference point.

rules: In a verb phrase, the auxiliaries always precede the main verb; the main verb always comes last in the chain.
Modals (will, shall, can, may, must, etc.) are followed by the bare infinitive (base form without 'to').
The auxiliary 'have' is followed by the past participle; the auxiliary 'be' is followed by the present participle (-ing) for progressive or past participle for passive.
Tense is marked only on the first word of the verb phrase (modal or first auxiliary), never on the main verb when auxiliaries are present.
In negative sentences, 'not' is inserted after the first auxiliary: 'has not been approved', 'could not have known'.
In questions, the first auxiliary is inverted with the subject: 'Has she been informed?' not 'She has been informed?'

examples.text: The committee has been reviewing the proposals for three weeks.
examples.note: 'has been reviewing' is the verb phrase: 'has' (auxiliary/perfect) + 'been' (auxiliary/progressive) + 'reviewing' (main verb).

examples.text: The budget will be announced next month.
examples.note: 'will be announced' — modal + passive: future passive verb phrase.

examples.text: She might not have submitted the form in time.
examples.note: 'might not have submitted' — modal + negative + perfect aspect.

examples.text: The suspect was being interrogated when the lawyer arrived.
examples.note: 'was being interrogated' — past progressive passive verb phrase.

examples.text: He could have been waiting for hours.
examples.note: 'could have been waiting' — modal + perfect + progressive (modal perfect progressive).

commonMistakes.wrong: She has wrote the report.
commonMistakes.right: She has written the report.
commonMistakes.note: After 'have/has', use the past participle ('written'), not the simple past ('wrote').

commonMistakes.wrong: He did not went to the office.
commonMistakes.right: He did not go to the office.
commonMistakes.note: After auxiliary 'did', use the bare infinitive (base form), not the past tense.

commonMistakes.wrong: They must to submit the form.
commonMistakes.right: They must submit the form.
commonMistakes.note: Modal verbs are followed by the bare infinitive, never 'to + verb'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The decision will announced tomorrow.
commonMistakes.right: The decision will be announced tomorrow.
commonMistakes.note: Passive voice requires 'be' before the past participle: 'will be announced'.

practice.question: Which sentence contains a verb phrase in the present perfect passive?
options: She has been waiting since morning.
They will have completed the task.
practice.explanation: 'Has been approved' = have + been (passive auxiliary) + past participle. This is present perfect passive. Option A is present perfect progressive (active).

practice.question: Identify the error in: 'The minister should has informed parliament.'
options: should has — modal must be followed by bare infinitive 'have'
practice.explanation: After a modal verb, the auxiliary 'have' must be in its base form: 'should have informed'.

practice.question: Which option correctly completes: 'By next year, he ___ in this department for a decade.'?
practice.explanation: The time marker 'By next year' signals the future perfect progressive: 'will have been working'.

quiz.question: In 'The results could not have been declared before verification', which part is the verb phrase?
quiz.explanation: 'Could not have been declared' is the complete verb phrase: modal + negative + perfect auxiliary + passive auxiliary + main verb.

quiz.question: Which sequence correctly describes the structure of 'was being examined'?
quiz.explanation: 'Was being examined' = past tense of 'be' + present participle of 'be' + past participle → past progressive passive.

quiz.question: Which rule is violated in: 'He has went to Karachi'?
options: Modal must be followed by bare infinitive.
'Have' must be followed by the past participle, not simple past.
quiz.explanation: After 'has', the past participle 'gone' is required, not the simple past form 'went'.

content.summary: A verb phrase consists of a main verb and its accompanying auxiliaries and/or modals, encoding tense, aspect, voice, and modality. The fixed order is: (modal) → (have + past participle) → (be + -ing/past participle) → main verb, with tense marked only on the first element. Common exam errors include using simple past after 'have', adding 'to' after modals, and omitting 'be' in passive constructions.

content.introduction: Future tense passive constructions are straightforward but require careful use of 'will be' or 'will have been'. Future Continuous and Future Perfect Continuous passive forms are not used in standard English. CSS and PMS exams frequently test Simple Future passive and Future Perfect passive.
content.urduExplanation: Future Tenses میں Passive Voice بنانے کے دو اہم طریقے ہیں۔ Simple Future میں 'will be + V3' یا 'shall be + V3' آتا ہے، جیسے 'She will write the letter' → 'The letter will be written by her'۔ Future Perfect میں 'will have been + V3' استعمال ہوتا ہے، جیسے 'They will have completed the project' → 'The project will have been completed by them'۔ Future Continuous اور Future Perfect Continuous کا Passive Voice عام طور پر نہیں بنایا جاتا اور انہیں امتحانات میں passive میں تبدیل کرنے کی کوشش نہیں کرنی چاہیے۔ 'Going to' کا Passive 'is/am/are going to be + V3' کی شکل میں بنتا ہے، جیسے 'They are going to build a hospital' → 'A hospital is going to be built by them'۔
content.englishExplanation: Future tenses have two primary passive forms in standard English. Simple Future Passive uses 'will be + V3' (or 'shall be + V3' in formal British usage). Formula: New subject + will be + V3 + (by + agent). Future Perfect Passive uses 'will have been + V3', indicating completion of an action before a future point. Formula: New subject + will have been + V3 + (by + agent). 'Going to' future also has a passive: 'is/am/are going to be + V3'. Future Continuous ('will be + V-ing') and Future Perfect Continuous ('will have been + V-ing') do not have standard passive forms and are not tested in this form. Negative future passive: insert 'not' after 'will' → 'will not be + V3'; 'will not have been + V3'.

types.name: Simple Future Passive
types.description: Active: S + will + V1 + O → Passive: O + will be + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'The company will launch a new product.' → 'A new product will be launched by the company.'

types.name: Future Perfect Passive
types.description: Active: S + will have + V3 + O → Passive: O + will have been + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'She will have finished the report by Monday.' → 'The report will have been finished by her by Monday.'

types.name: 'Going to' Future Passive
types.description: Active: S + is/am/are going to + V1 + O → Passive: O + is/am/are going to be + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'They are going to renovate the office.' → 'The office is going to be renovated by them.'

types.name: Future Continuous & Future Perfect Continuous (No Passive)
types.description: Future Continuous ('will be V-ing') and Future Perfect Continuous ('will have been V-ing') do not form standard passive constructions. Avoid converting them to passive.

types.name: Negative Simple Future Passive
types.description: Active: S + will not + V1 + O → Passive: O + will not be + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'He will not sign the document.' → 'The document will not be signed by him.'

rules: Simple Future passive: will be + V3. 'Will' is invariable for all subjects.
Future Perfect passive: will have been + V3. The time reference is retained after the verb phrase.
'Going to' future passive: is/am/are going to be + V3.
Future Continuous and Future Perfect Continuous do not have standard passive forms — do not attempt to passivise them.
Negative future passive: 'will not be + V3'; the contraction 'won't be + V3' is also acceptable in informal contexts.
The past participle (V3) must be correct regardless of the future auxiliary used.
Time expressions ('by next Monday', 'soon', 'before noon') are retained in the passive sentence.

examples.text: Active: The government will build a new highway. / Passive: A new highway will be built by the government.
examples.note: Simple Future passive: 'will build' → 'will be built'. 'A new highway' becomes the subject.

examples.text: Active: She will have submitted the report by Friday. / Passive: The report will have been submitted by her by Friday.
examples.note: Future Perfect passive: 'will have submitted' → 'will have been submitted'. 'She' → 'her'. Time phrase retained.

examples.text: Active: They are going to announce the results tomorrow. / Passive: The results are going to be announced by them tomorrow.
examples.note: 'Going to' passive: 'are going to announce' → 'are going to be announced'.

examples.text: Active: The company will not refund the money. / Passive: The money will not be refunded by the company.
examples.note: Negative Simple Future: 'will not refund' → 'will not be refunded'.

examples.text: Active: Scientists will have discovered a cure by 2030. / Passive: A cure will have been discovered by scientists by 2030.
examples.note: Future Perfect: 'will have discovered' → 'will have been discovered'. Time phrase 'by 2030' retained.

commonMistakes.wrong: The letter will written by her.
commonMistakes.right: The letter will be written by her.
commonMistakes.note: The auxiliary 'be' cannot be omitted in Simple Future passive. Must have 'will be + V3'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The project will have been complete by the team.
commonMistakes.right: The project will have been completed by the team.
commonMistakes.note: After 'will have been', the past participle V3 is required: 'complete' → 'completed'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The report will be being written by her.
commonMistakes.right: Rephrase: The report will be written by her. (Future Continuous has no standard passive.)
commonMistakes.note: Future Continuous passive is not standard. Use Simple Future passive instead.

commonMistakes.wrong: A hospital will going to be built by them.
commonMistakes.right: A hospital is going to be built by them.
commonMistakes.note: 'Going to' passive uses 'is/am/are going to be + V3', not 'will going to be'.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'The authorities will announce the decision tomorrow.'
options: The decision will be announced by the authorities tomorrow.
The decision will have been announced by the authorities tomorrow.
The decision is announced by the authorities tomorrow.
The decision would be announced by the authorities tomorrow.
practice.explanation: Simple Future passive: 'will announce' → 'will be announced'. Time adverb 'tomorrow' is retained. Option a is correct.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'She will have completed the task before noon.'
options: The task will be completed by her before noon.
The task has been completed by her before noon.
The task will have been completed by her before noon.
The task had been completed by her before noon.
practice.explanation: Future Perfect passive: 'will have completed' → 'will have been completed'. 'She' → 'her'. Time phrase retained. Option c is correct.

practice.question: Active: 'They are going to repair the road.' Which passive is correct?
options: The road will be repaired by them.
The road is going to be repaired by them.
The road is going to been repaired by them.
The road was going to be repaired by them.
practice.explanation: 'Going to' passive: 'are going to repair' → 'is going to be repaired'. 'Road' is singular; 'is'. Option b is correct.

quiz.question: Which passive form is correct for Simple Future tense?
quiz.explanation: Simple Future passive requires 'will be + V3'. Option a omits 'be'; option c has wrong form; option d is Future Perfect passive.

quiz.question: Active: 'Scientists will have found a vaccine.' Correct passive: ___
options: A vaccine will be found by scientists.
A vaccine has been found by scientists.
A vaccine will have been found by scientists.
A vaccine would have been found by scientists.
quiz.explanation: Future Perfect active 'will have found' → Future Perfect passive 'will have been found'. Option c is correct.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly converts Future Continuous to passive?
options: The project will be being finished by them.
The project will have been finished by them.
The project will be finished by them. (Rephrase — Future Continuous has no standard passive.)
The project was being finished by them.
quiz.explanation: Future Continuous ('will be finishing') has no standard passive form. The best approach is to rephrase as Simple Future passive: 'will be finished'.

content.summary: Future tense passives use: Simple Future → will be + V3; Future Perfect → will have been + V3; 'Going to' future → is/am/are going to be + V3. Future Continuous and Future Perfect Continuous have no standard passive forms. Always retain time expressions and use the correct past participle (V3).

content.introduction: Imperative sentences express commands, orders, requests, or advice. They have no stated subject — the subject 'you' is implied. Converting imperative sentences to passive voice is a unique and frequently tested skill in Pakistani competitive exams.
content.urduExplanation: Imperative Sentences وہ جملے ہوتے ہیں جن میں حکم، درخواست یا مشورہ دیا جاتا ہے، اور ان کا Subject 'you' چھپا ہوتا ہے۔ ان کا Passive بنانے کے دو طریقے ہیں: پہلا طریقہ: 'Let + Object + be + V3'، جیسے 'Open the door' → 'Let the door be opened'۔ دوسرا طریقہ: 'You are requested/advised/ordered to + V1 + Object'، جیسے 'Please sit down' → 'You are requested to sit down'۔ منفی حکم (Don't/Never) کی صورت میں: 'Let + Object + not + be + V3'، جیسے 'Don't waste time' → 'Let time not be wasted'۔ یاد رہے کہ Imperative کا Subject 'you' Passive میں عام طور پر ظاہر نہیں ہوتا۔
content.englishExplanation: Imperative sentences are commands or requests where the subject 'you' is understood but not stated. Because there is no explicit object that becomes the subject in the usual way, imperative passives use two specialised patterns. Pattern 1 – 'Let + object + be + V3': This is the primary exam-accepted form. The object of the active command becomes the focus, introduced by 'let'. Example: 'Shut the window.' → 'Let the window be shut.' Pattern 2 – 'You are requested/advised/ordered/told to + V1 + (object)': Used when expressing polite requests or formal orders. Example: 'Please submit your forms.' → 'You are requested to submit your forms.' Negative imperatives ('Do not', 'Never', 'Don't') are converted as: 'Let + object + not + be + V3' or 'You are advised/requested not to + V1'. Example: 'Don't litter the streets.' → 'Let the streets not be littered.' OR 'You are requested not to litter the streets.' The choice of 'requested', 'advised', 'ordered', or 'told' depends on the tone and context of the original command.

types.name: Pattern 1: Let + Object + be + V3
types.description: The primary passive form for imperatives. Active: 'V1 + object.' → Passive: 'Let + object + be + V3.' Example: 'Close the door.' → 'Let the door be closed.'

types.name: Pattern 2: You are requested/advised/ordered to + V1
types.description: Used for polite or formal requests. Example: 'Please help the poor.' → 'You are requested to help the poor.' OR 'The poor should be helped.'

types.name: Negative Imperative Passive (Pattern 1)
types.description: Active: 'Do not / Never + V1 + object.' → Passive: 'Let + object + not + be + V3.' Example: 'Don't waste water.' → 'Let water not be wasted.'

types.name: Negative Imperative Passive (Pattern 2)
types.description: Active: 'Do not + V1 + object.' → Passive: 'You are requested/advised not to + V1 + object.' Example: 'Do not make noise.' → 'You are requested not to make noise.'

types.name: Choosing the Right Verb (requested / advised / ordered / told)
types.description: Use 'requested' for polite requests, 'advised' for suggestions, 'ordered' or 'commanded' for strong directives, 'told' for instructions.

rules: The primary passive of an imperative is: Let + object + be + V3.
An alternative form is: You are requested/advised/ordered/told to + V1 + (object).
For negative imperatives ('Do not/Never + V1'): Let + object + not + be + V3 OR You are requested/advised not to + V1.
The implied subject 'you' is NOT written as 'by you' in the passive of imperatives — it is omitted.
Select 'requested', 'advised', 'ordered', or 'told' based on the strength and formality of the original command.
If the imperative has no direct object (e.g., 'Go away', 'Sit down'), it generally cannot be passivised using Pattern 1; use Pattern 2 instead.
The past participle (V3) must be correctly formed after 'be' in Pattern 1.

examples.text: Active: Open the window. / Passive: Let the window be opened.
examples.note: Pattern 1: 'the window' becomes subject of 'let' construction; 'open' → 'be opened'.

examples.text: Active: Help the poor. / Passive: Let the poor be helped. / OR: You are requested to help the poor.
examples.note: Both Pattern 1 and Pattern 2 are acceptable. Pattern 2 uses 'requested' for a polite tone.

examples.text: Active: Do not waste time. / Passive: Let time not be wasted. / OR: You are advised not to waste time.
examples.note: Negative imperative: 'not' is placed after 'Let + object' or after 'not to' in Pattern 2.

examples.text: Active: Never tell a lie. / Passive: Let a lie never be told. / OR: You are advised never to tell a lie.
examples.note: Adverb 'never' is retained and placed appropriately in the passive.

examples.text: Active: Please submit your application. / Passive: You are requested to submit your application.
examples.note: Polite imperative with 'please': use 'requested'. Pattern 2 is most natural here.

examples.text: Active: Follow the traffic rules. / Passive: Let the traffic rules be followed. / OR: You are ordered to follow the traffic rules.
examples.note: Both patterns work; 'ordered' suits a directive context.

commonMistakes.wrong: Let the door be close.
commonMistakes.right: Let the door be closed.
commonMistakes.note: After 'be' in passive, the past participle V3 is required: 'close' (V1) → 'closed' (V3).

commonMistakes.wrong: Let not be wasted time.
commonMistakes.right: Let time not be wasted.
commonMistakes.note: The object must immediately follow 'let': 'Let + object (time) + not + be + V3'.

commonMistakes.wrong: You are requested to not make noise.
commonMistakes.right: You are requested not to make noise.
commonMistakes.note: In formal English, 'not' precedes 'to' in the infinitive: 'not to make', not 'to not make'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Let the children be played. (Active: 'Play, children!')
commonMistakes.right: Let the children play. (This is already a 'let' sentence, not a passive.)
commonMistakes.note: When the imperative begins with 'Let + noun + V1', it is already a permission/suggestion — do not add 'be' unless converting to passive.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'Clean the room immediately.'
options: Let the room be cleaned immediately.
Let the room be clean immediately.
The room must be cleaned immediately.
You are advised to clean the room immediately.
practice.explanation: Pattern 1 imperative passive: 'Let + the room + be + cleaned'. V3 of 'clean' is 'cleaned'. Adverb 'immediately' is retained. Both a and d are acceptable but a is the primary exam answer. Option a is the most standard Pattern 1 response.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'Do not park your car here.'
options: Let your car not parked here.
Let your car not be parked here.
You are requested to not park your car here.
Your car must not be parked here.
practice.explanation: Negative imperative Pattern 1: 'Let + your car + not + be + parked'. V3 of 'park' is 'parked'. Option b is correct. Option c has incorrect infinitive placement.

practice.question: Which is the most appropriate passive for: 'Please respect your teachers.'?
options: You are requested to respect your teachers.
Both a and b are acceptable.
practice.explanation: Both Pattern 1 ('Let your teachers be respected') and Pattern 2 ('You are requested to respect your teachers') are grammatically correct passives for a polite imperative. Option d is correct.

quiz.question: Identify the correct passive of: 'Never break the law.'
options: The law should never be broken.
Let the law never be broken.
Let the law not be broken never.
You are requested to never break the law.
quiz.explanation: Imperative Pattern 1: 'Let + the law + never + be + broken'. 'Never' is placed before 'be'. Option b is the most standard exam answer.

quiz.question: Active: 'Switch off the lights before leaving.' Passive (Pattern 1): ___
options: Let the lights be switched off before leaving.
Let the lights be switch off before leaving.
Let the lights are switched off before leaving.
The lights should be switched off before leaving.
quiz.explanation: Pattern 1: 'Let + the lights + be + switched off'. V3 of 'switch off' is 'switched off'. Time phrase retained. Option a is correct.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the Pattern 2 passive of: 'Obey the orders.'?
options: You are ordered to obey the orders.
The orders are to be obeyed.
Orders must be obeyed by you.
quiz.explanation: Pattern 2: 'You are ordered/requested to + V1 + object'. 'Obey the orders' → 'You are ordered to obey the orders.' Option b is Pattern 2.

content.summary: Imperative sentences convert to passive using two patterns: Pattern 1 – 'Let + object + be + V3' (primary form); Pattern 2 – 'You are requested/advised/ordered to + V1 + object'. Negative imperatives use 'Let + object + not + be + V3' or 'You are advised/requested not to + V1'. The implied subject 'you' is not written as agent in imperative passives.

content.introduction: Interrogative sentences (questions) can be converted to passive voice, but the question structure must be preserved. Yes/No questions (using auxiliaries) and Wh-questions each have their own passive conversion pattern. The most tested form on competitive exams is the 'Who/Whom' question conversion.
content.urduExplanation: سوالیہ جملوں کو Passive Voice میں تبدیل کرنا ذرا مختلف ہوتا ہے لیکن قابل فہم ہے۔ Yes/No سوالات میں Auxiliary Verb (helping verb) کو آگے رکھا جاتا ہے، جیسے 'Did she write the letter?' → 'Was the letter written by her?'۔ Wh-Questions میں Wh-Word کو آگے رکھا جاتا ہے، جیسے 'What did he buy?' → 'What was bought by him?'۔ خاص اہمیت 'Who' سوالات کی ہے: 'Who wrote this letter?' → 'By whom was this letter written?' یا 'Who was this letter written by?'۔ یاد رہے کہ Passive Question میں بھی سوالیہ شکل (inversion) برقرار رہتی ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Interrogative passive sentences maintain the question word order: auxiliary verb before subject. For Yes/No questions, the structure is: Passive auxiliary (is/are/was/were/will be + V3) + new subject + (by + agent) + ? For Wh-questions (what, which, when, where, why, how), the Wh-word is placed first, followed by the passive auxiliary inversion. The most important special case is 'Who' questions: 'Who' as subject of an active question converts to 'By whom' in passive (formal) or 'Who ... by?' (informal). Formula for 'Who' questions: Active: 'Who + V2 + object?' → Passive: 'By whom + was/were + object + V3?' For 'Whom' as object in active: 'Whom did she invite?' → 'Who was invited by her?' — here 'whom' (old object) becomes the new subject 'who'. The tense of the passive auxiliary must match the tense of the original active question.

types.name: Yes/No Question Passive
types.description: Active: Auxiliary + subject + V1 + object? → Passive: Passive auxiliary (was/were/is/are + V3) + new subject + by + agent? Example: 'Did he solve the problem?' → 'Was the problem solved by him?'

types.name: Wh-Question Passive (Object Wh-word)
types.description: Active: Wh-word (as object) + auxiliary + subject + V1? → Passive: Wh-word + passive auxiliary + new subject + V3 + by + agent? Example: 'What did she buy?' → 'What was bought by her?'

types.name: 'Who' as Subject (Active) → 'By whom' (Passive)
types.description: Active: 'Who + V2 + object?' → Passive: 'By whom + was/were + object + V3?' (formal) OR 'Who was [object] V3 by?' (informal). Example: 'Who wrote this letter?' → 'By whom was this letter written?'

types.name: 'Whom' as Object (Active) → 'Who' as Subject (Passive)
types.description: Active: 'Whom did + subject + V1?' → Passive: 'Who + was/were + V3 + by + agent?' Example: 'Whom did the teacher punish?' → 'Who was punished by the teacher?'

types.name: Wh-Question with Subject Wh-word (What/Which)
types.description: Active: 'What + V2 + object?' → Passive retains 'What' and inverts: 'What + was/were + V3 + by + agent?' Example: 'What surprised him?' → 'By what was he surprised?' (formal) or 'What was he surprised by?'

rules: The question form (inversion of auxiliary and subject) must be preserved in the passive.
Yes/No questions: replace active auxiliary with passive auxiliary (was/were/is/are + V3) and maintain question order.
'Who' as active subject → 'By whom' at the start of the passive question (formal) or 'Who ... by?' (informal).
'Whom' as active object → becomes 'Who' (new subject) at the start of the passive question.
For Wh-questions where the Wh-word is the object, keep it at the front and convert the rest: 'What did he bring?' → 'What was brought by him?'
Tense of the passive auxiliary must match the tense of the original question auxiliary.
The question mark (?) must be retained in all passive interrogative sentences.

examples.text: Active: Did she write the letter? / Passive: Was the letter written by her?
examples.note: Simple Past Yes/No: 'Did + she + write' → 'Was + the letter + written'. 'she' → 'her'.

examples.text: Active: Who broke the window? / Passive: By whom was the window broken?
examples.note: 'Who' (active subject) → 'By whom' at the start. Simple Past passive.

examples.text: Active: What did the manager say? / Passive: What was said by the manager?
examples.note: Wh-word 'What' is the object in active; retained at front. 'did say' → 'was said'.

examples.text: Active: Whom did the officer arrest? / Passive: Who was arrested by the officer?
examples.note: 'Whom' (active object) → 'Who' (new passive subject) at the front.

examples.text: Active: Will the government build a new hospital? / Passive: Will a new hospital be built by the government?
examples.note: Future Yes/No question: 'will build' → 'will be built'. Inversion maintained.

examples.text: Active: Has she completed the assignment? / Passive: Has the assignment been completed by her?
examples.note: Present Perfect question: 'has completed' → 'has been completed'. 'she' → 'her'.

commonMistakes.wrong: Was the letter written by she?
commonMistakes.right: Was the letter written by her?
commonMistakes.note: After 'by', use object pronouns: 'she' → 'her'.

commonMistakes.wrong: By who was the letter written?
commonMistakes.right: By whom was the letter written?
commonMistakes.note: After a preposition like 'by', the objective form 'whom' is used in formal/exam English, not 'who'.

commonMistakes.wrong: What did he buy? → What was bought?
commonMistakes.right: What was bought by him?
commonMistakes.note: The agent 'by him' is important information from the original sentence and should be retained if the original subject is specific.

commonMistakes.wrong: Did the problem solve by him?
commonMistakes.right: Was the problem solved by him?
commonMistakes.note: Passive of a Simple Past question uses 'was/were + V3', not the active auxiliary 'did'.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'Did the police catch the criminal?'
options: Was the criminal caught by the police?
Was the criminal catched by the police?
Is the criminal caught by the police?
Did the criminal caught by the police?
practice.explanation: Simple Past Yes/No passive: 'Did + catch' → 'Was + caught' (V3). Singular 'criminal' takes 'was'. Option a is correct. 'catched' in b is wrong (V3 of 'catch' is 'caught').

practice.question: Change to passive: 'Who wrote this poem?'
options: Who was this poem written by?
By whom was this poem written?
By who was this poem written?
Both a and b are acceptable.
practice.explanation: Both 'By whom was this poem written?' (formal) and 'Who was this poem written by?' (informal/acceptable) are correct. Option d is the best answer. Option c ('By who') is incorrect; 'by' requires 'whom'.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'Whom did the teacher scold?'
options: By whom was the teacher scolded?
Who was scolded by the teacher?
Whom was scolded by the teacher?
practice.explanation: 'Whom' is the object in the active question — it becomes the new subject 'Who' (subjective case) in the passive. Passive: 'Who was scolded by the teacher?' Option b is correct.

quiz.question: Active: 'Has the committee reviewed the proposal?' Passive: ___
options: Has the proposal reviewed by the committee?
Has the proposal been reviewed by the committee?
Was the proposal reviewed by the committee?
Is the proposal been reviewed by the committee?
quiz.explanation: Present Perfect Yes/No question: 'Has + reviewed' → 'Has + been + reviewed'. Auxiliary 'has' is retained and inverted. Option b is correct.

quiz.question: Active: 'What did she say?' Passive: ___
options: What had been said by her?
By what was said by her?
quiz.explanation: 'What' is the object in active; it stays at the front in passive. 'did say' (Simple Past) → 'was said'. 'she' → 'her'. Option a is correct.

quiz.question: Which passive of 'Who built the Taj Mahal?' is most formal and grammatically preferred?
options: Who was the Taj Mahal built by?
By whom the Taj Mahal was built?
By whom was the Taj Mahal built?
Whom was the Taj Mahal built by?
quiz.explanation: Formal passive: 'By whom + was + subject + V3?' Option c maintains correct inversion and uses formal 'By whom' at the start. Option b lacks inversion. Options a and d are less formal or incorrect.

content.summary: Interrogative passive sentences maintain question word order (auxiliary before subject). Yes/No questions: replace active auxiliary with passive auxiliary (was/were/is/are/will be + V3). 'Who' as active subject becomes 'By whom' at the start of the formal passive question. 'Whom' as active object becomes 'Who' as the new passive subject. Wh-word objects are retained at the front, and all question marks are preserved.

content.introduction: Voice is a grammatical category that describes the relationship between the verb and its subject and object. In active voice, the subject performs the action. In passive voice, the subject receives the action. Understanding voice is essential for CSS, PMS, IELTS, and all competitive exams in Pakistan.
content.urduExplanation: Voice گرامر کی وہ اصطلاح ہے جو فعل اور فاعل کے درمیان تعلق کو ظاہر کرتی ہے۔ Active Voice میں فاعل (Subject) خود کام کرتا ہے، جیسے 'Ali writes a letter'۔ Passive Voice میں فاعل کام کرنے والا نہیں بلکہ کام سہنے والا ہوتا ہے، جیسے 'A letter is written by Ali'۔ Passive Voice اس وقت استعمال ہوتی ہے جب کام کرنے والا معلوم نہ ہو یا اہم نہ ہو، یا جب سرکاری، سائنسی یا رسمی تحریر لکھنی ہو۔ Object کو Subject کی جگہ پر رکھا جاتا ہے اور فعل کی شکل 'be + past participle' میں بدل جاتی ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Voice in English grammar refers to the form of a verb that shows whether the subject performs or receives the action. In active voice, the subject is the doer: 'The manager signed the contract.' In passive voice, the subject is the receiver: 'The contract was signed by the manager.' Passive voice is preferred when the agent (doer) is unknown ('My wallet was stolen'), unimportant, or deliberately withheld for style. It is heavily used in scientific writing ('The experiment was conducted'), official documents, and journalistic reporting. The fundamental transformation rule is: the object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence, the verb changes to the appropriate form of 'be' plus the past participle (V3), and the original subject becomes the agent introduced by 'by'.

types.name: Active Voice
types.description: The subject performs the action. Structure: Subject + Verb + Object. Example: 'The teacher explains the lesson.'

types.name: Passive Voice
types.description: The subject receives the action. Structure: Object (new subject) + be + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'The lesson is explained by the teacher.'

types.name: When Agent is Unknown
types.description: If the doer is unknown or unimportant, the 'by + agent' phrase is omitted. Example: 'The window was broken.' (we do not know who broke it)

types.name: Formal / Scientific Passive
