types.description: Academic and official writing frequently uses passive to maintain objectivity. Example: 'The results were analysed.' / 'The policy was reviewed.'

rules: The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive sentence.
The verb changes to 'be' (in the appropriate tense) + past participle (V3).
The original subject becomes the agent, introduced by 'by' (e.g., 'by Ali', 'by the government').
If the agent is unknown, unimportant, or obvious from context, 'by + agent' may be omitted.
Only transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) can be converted to passive voice.
The tense of the auxiliary 'be' must match the tense of the original active verb.
Subject pronouns change to object pronouns when they become agents: I→me, he→him, she→her, they→them, we→us.

examples.text: Active: She writes a letter. / Passive: A letter is written by her.
examples.note: 'a letter' (object) becomes the subject; 'writes' becomes 'is written'; 'she' becomes 'her'.

examples.text: Active: The police arrested the thief. / Passive: The thief was arrested by the police.
examples.note: 'the thief' moves to subject position; 'arrested' becomes 'was arrested'.

examples.text: Active: Someone broke the window. / Passive: The window was broken.
examples.note: 'Someone' is vague, so 'by someone' is omitted in the passive.

examples.text: Active: They will announce the results. / Passive: The results will be announced (by them).
examples.note: Future tense: 'will announce' → 'will be announced'.

examples.text: Active: People speak English all over the world. / Passive: English is spoken all over the world.
examples.note: 'People' is a general agent and is typically omitted.

commonMistakes.wrong: The letter was wrote by her.
commonMistakes.right: The letter was written by her.
commonMistakes.note: 'wrote' is simple past, not past participle. Use V3 ('written') after 'be'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The cake eaten by him.
commonMistakes.right: The cake was eaten by him.
commonMistakes.note: The auxiliary verb 'be' (here 'was') must not be omitted in passive constructions.

commonMistakes.wrong: He was written a letter by her.
commonMistakes.right: A letter was written to him by her. / He was given a letter by her.
commonMistakes.note: With ditransitive verbs, restructure carefully; 'write' does not passivise the indirect object this way.

commonMistakes.wrong: The work is doing by him.
commonMistakes.right: The work is being done by him.
commonMistakes.note: Present Continuous passive requires 'is/am/are being + V3', not 'is doing'.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'Ali reads the newspaper every morning.'
options: The newspaper is read by Ali every morning.
The newspaper was read by Ali every morning.
The newspaper has been read by Ali every morning.
The newspaper is being read by Ali every morning.
practice.explanation: Simple Present active uses 'reads'; passive uses 'is + read (V3)'. Result: 'The newspaper is read by Ali every morning.'

practice.question: Which sentence is correctly converted to passive voice? Active: 'The government announced new policies.'
options: New policies announced by the government.
New policies were announced by the government.
New policies are announced by the government.
New policies have announced by the government.
practice.explanation: 'announced' is Simple Past; passive requires 'were + announced (V3)'. Option b is correct.

practice.question: Why is passive voice preferred in: 'Mistakes were made'?
options: Because the agent is unknown or deliberately withheld
Because it is always more polite
practice.explanation: Passive is used here to avoid naming the agent — the doer of 'mistakes' is unknown or the writer prefers not to assign blame.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a correct passive sentence?
options: The book was read by he.
The book was read by him.
The book were read by him.
The book is read by him yesterday.
quiz.explanation: After 'by', subject pronouns change to object form: 'he' → 'him'. 'was read' is correct Simple Past passive. Options a, c, and d each contain errors.

quiz.question: Active: 'No one has solved this problem.' Which passive is correct?
options: This problem has not been solved by anyone.
This problem was not solved by no one.
This problem is not solved by anyone.
This problem had not been solved by anyone.
quiz.explanation: Present Perfect active ('has solved') → passive 'has been solved'. 'No one' becomes 'by anyone' (avoid double negative). Tense stays Present Perfect.

quiz.question: Intransitive verbs (verbs without an object) ______ be converted to passive voice.
quiz.explanation: Passive voice requires an object to move to the subject position. Intransitive verbs like 'sleep', 'arrive', 'go' have no object, so they cannot form a passive.

content.summary: Voice describes whether the subject acts (active) or is acted upon (passive). Converting active to passive involves moving the object to the subject position, changing the verb to 'be + V3' in the same tense, and placing the original subject after 'by'. Passive is preferred when the agent is unknown, unimportant, or in formal and scientific contexts.

content.introduction: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would, ought to) express necessity, possibility, permission, or ability. All modals follow the same passive pattern: modal + be + past participle (V3). Modal passives are extensively tested in CSS, PMS, and IELTS writing and grammar sections.
content.urduExplanation: Modal Verbs جیسے can, could, may, might, must, should, would وغیرہ کے ساتھ Passive Voice بنانا بہت آسان ہے۔ فارمولا ہمیشہ یہی رہتا ہے: Modal + be + V3 (past participle)۔ مثال کے طور پر: 'She can solve this problem' → 'This problem can be solved by her'۔ 'You must obey the rules' → 'The rules must be obeyed by you'۔ 'They should complete the report' → 'The report should be completed by them'۔ یاد رہے کہ Modal کے بعد ہمیشہ 'be' آتا ہے، نہ کہ 'been' یا 'being'، اور پھر V3 لگتی ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: Passive voice with modal verbs follows a single universal formula regardless of which modal is used. Active Formula: Subject + modal + base verb (V1) + object. Passive Formula: Object (new subject) + modal + be + V3 + (by + agent). The word 'be' is always in base form after the modal — never 'been' or 'being' (those are reserved for perfect and progressive constructions). For 'ought to', the passive is: ought to be + V3. Negative modal passives insert 'not' between the modal and 'be': 'cannot be done', 'should not be ignored', 'must not be wasted'. Perfect modals ('could have done', 'should have done') also passivise: 'could have been done', 'should have been completed'. This is an important distinction: simple modal passive uses 'modal + be + V3'; perfect modal passive uses 'modal + have + been + V3'.

types.name: Simple Modal Passive
types.description: Active: S + modal + V1 + O → Passive: O + modal + be + V3 + by + agent. Works for: can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would. Example: 'She can finish it.' → 'It can be finished by her.'

types.name: Negative Modal Passive
types.description: Active: S + modal + not + V1 + O → Passive: O + modal + not + be + V3. Example: 'You must not waste time.' → 'Time must not be wasted.' (agent 'by you' is omitted as it is obvious).

types.name: 'Ought to' Passive
types.description: Active: S + ought to + V1 + O → Passive: O + ought to be + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'We ought to respect our elders.' → 'Our elders ought to be respected by us.'

types.name: Perfect Modal Passive
types.description: Active: S + modal + have + V3 + O → Passive: O + modal + have + been + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'She should have submitted the form.' → 'The form should have been submitted by her.'

types.name: Common Modal Passive Forms Quick Reference
types.description: can be done | could be done | may be done | might be done | must be done | should be done | would be done | will be done | shall be done | ought to be done

rules: Universal modal passive formula: modal + be + V3. The base verb 'be' never changes after a modal.
Do NOT use 'been' or 'being' directly after a modal in simple modal passive (those are for perfect/continuous forms).
Negative modal passive: modal + not + be + V3 (e.g., 'cannot be used', 'should not be ignored').
Perfect modal passive: modal + have + been + V3 (e.g., 'could have been done', 'must have been completed').
'Ought to' passive: ought to be + V3 (same formula, but note the 'to' is retained).
The agent 'by + noun/pronoun' is retained when important; omit when vague, obvious, or unknown.
Subject pronoun becomes object pronoun if retained as agent: he→him, she→her, they→them, we→us, I→me.

examples.text: Active: The doctor can treat this disease. / Passive: This disease can be treated by the doctor.
examples.note: 'can treat' → 'can be treated'. Object 'this disease' becomes new subject.

examples.text: Active: Students must complete the assignment. / Passive: The assignment must be completed by the students.
examples.note: 'must complete' → 'must be completed'. Singular 'assignment' with 'be'.

examples.text: Active: You should not waste water. / Passive: Water should not be wasted.
examples.note: Negative: 'should not waste' → 'should not be wasted'. 'You' is obvious agent, omitted.

examples.text: Active: The government may review the policy. / Passive: The policy may be reviewed by the government.
examples.note: 'may review' → 'may be reviewed'. Possibility maintained.

examples.text: Active: He could have prevented the accident. / Passive: The accident could have been prevented by him.
examples.note: Perfect modal passive: 'could have prevented' → 'could have been prevented'. 'He' → 'him'.

examples.text: Active: We ought to preserve our national heritage. / Passive: Our national heritage ought to be preserved by us.
examples.note: 'ought to preserve' → 'ought to be preserved'. 'To' is retained with 'ought'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The work can been done by him.
commonMistakes.right: The work can be done by him.
commonMistakes.note: After a modal, always use the base form 'be', not 'been'. 'been' is for perfect constructions.

commonMistakes.wrong: The problem must be solve immediately.
commonMistakes.right: The problem must be solved immediately.
commonMistakes.note: After 'be' in passive, always use the past participle V3 ('solved'), not V1 ('solve').

commonMistakes.wrong: The rules should have be followed.
commonMistakes.right: The rules should have been followed.
commonMistakes.note: Perfect modal passive: 'modal + have + been + V3'. 'be' must be 'been' here.

commonMistakes.wrong: This ought be respected.
commonMistakes.right: This ought to be respected.
commonMistakes.note: 'Ought' always requires 'to' before the following verb: 'ought to be + V3'.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'You should finish the work before sunset.'
options: The work should be finished before sunset by you.
The work must be finished before sunset by you.
The work should have been finished before sunset by you.
The work will be finished before sunset by you.
practice.explanation: Modal passive: 'should finish' → 'should be finished'. 'You' retained as agent. Time expression preserved. Option a is correct.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'They could have solved this problem easily.'
options: This problem could be solved easily by them.
This problem could have been solved easily by them.
This problem could have solved easily by them.
This problem should have been solved easily by them.
practice.explanation: Perfect modal passive: 'could have solved' → 'could have been solved'. Adverb 'easily' is retained. Option b is correct.

practice.question: Active: 'We must not pollute the environment.' Which passive is correct?
options: The environment must not be polluted by us.
The environment must not pollute by us.
The environment can not be polluted by us.
The environment must not been polluted by us.
practice.explanation: Negative modal passive: 'must not pollute' → 'must not be polluted'. Option a correctly uses 'must not be + V3'.

quiz.question: Which is the correct passive of: 'The manager might approve the proposal'?
options: The proposal might be approved by the manager.
The proposal might been approved by the manager.
The proposal might have approved by the manager.
The proposal may be approving by the manager.
quiz.explanation: Simple modal passive: 'might approve' → 'might be approved'. V3 'approved' is correct. Option a is correct.

quiz.question: Active: 'She should have informed the committee.' Passive: ___
options: The committee should be informed by her.
The committee should have been informed by her.
The committee must have been informed by her.
The committee should have be informed by her.
quiz.explanation: Perfect modal passive: 'should have informed' → 'should have been informed'. Option b is correct. Option d wrongly uses 'be' instead of 'been'.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'ought to' passive?
options: The poor ought be helped by the rich.
The poor ought to been helped by the rich.
The poor ought to have help by the rich.
The poor ought to be helped by the rich.
quiz.explanation: 'Ought to' passive requires 'ought to be + V3'. Option d is correct. Options a (missing 'to'), b (wrong 'been'), and c (wrong 'have help') all have structural errors.

content.summary: All modal verbs follow the same passive pattern: modal + be + V3. Negative modal passives insert 'not' between the modal and 'be'. Perfect modal passives use 'modal + have + been + V3'. 'Ought to' retains its 'to': ought to be + V3. Never use 'been' or 'being' directly after a modal in a simple modal passive.

content.introduction: Past tense passive constructions are among the most tested voice conversion topics in CSS, PMS, and IELTS. Each past sub-tense has a specific passive formula using 'was/were' or 'had been' as the auxiliary. Past Perfect Continuous passive is not standard and is avoided in formal writing.
content.urduExplanation: Past Tenses میں Passive Voice تین طریقوں سے بنتی ہے۔ Simple Past میں 'was/were + V3' آتا ہے، جیسے 'He wrote the letter' → 'The letter was written by him'۔ Past Continuous میں 'was/were + being + V3' استعمال ہوتا ہے، جیسے 'She was cooking food' → 'Food was being cooked by her'۔ Past Perfect میں 'had + been + V3' لگتا ہے، جیسے 'They had finished the work' → 'The work had been finished by them'۔ Past Perfect Continuous کا Passive نہیں بنتا — یہ اصول یاد رکھیں کیونکہ یہ امتحانات میں ایک عام غلطی ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: The three standard past passive forms correspond to Simple Past, Past Continuous, and Past Perfect. Simple Past Passive uses 'was/were + V3'. 'Was' is used with singular subjects (I, he, she, it, singular nouns); 'were' is used with plural subjects (we, they, plural nouns) and 'you'. Formula: New subject + was/were + V3 + (by + agent). Past Continuous Passive uses 'was/were + being + V3', signalling that an action was ongoing at a past moment. Formula: New subject + was/were + being + V3 + (by + agent). Past Perfect Passive uses 'had + been + V3', indicating that the action was completed before another past event. Formula: New subject + had + been + V3 + (by + agent). Past Perfect Continuous passive ('had been being + V3') is not used in standard English — rephrase using Past Perfect passive.

types.name: Simple Past Passive
types.description: Active: S + V2 + O → Passive: O + was/were + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'The manager signed the letter.' → 'The letter was signed by the manager.'

types.name: Past Continuous Passive
types.description: Active: S + was/were + V-ing + O → Passive: O + was/were + being + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'Workers were building the bridge.' → 'The bridge was being built by the workers.'

types.name: Past Perfect Passive
types.description: Active: S + had + V3 + O → Passive: O + had + been + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'She had completed the project before the deadline.' → 'The project had been completed by her before the deadline.'

types.name: Past Perfect Continuous (No Passive Form)
types.description: Past Perfect Continuous ('had been V-ing') has no standard passive form. Avoid it. If needed, rephrase using Past Perfect passive.

types.name: was vs. were in Simple Past Passive
types.description: 'Was' → singular new subject (I, he, she, it, singular noun). 'Were' → plural new subject (they, we, you, plural noun). Example: 'The book was read.' vs. 'The books were read.'

rules: Simple Past passive: was/were + V3. Use 'was' for singular, 'were' for plural new subjects.
Past Continuous passive: was/were + being + V3. Never omit 'being'.
Past Perfect passive: had + been + V3. 'Had' is invariable for all subjects in Past Perfect.
Past Perfect Continuous has no standard passive form; it must be rephrased.
The past participle (V3) is the same form regardless of whether the tense is Simple Past, Continuous, or Perfect passive.
Negative: insert 'not' after the first auxiliary: 'was not written', 'were not being repaired', 'had not been sent'.
Time expressions and adverbs of the active sentence are retained in the passive.

examples.text: Active: The police caught the thief. / Passive: The thief was caught by the police.
examples.note: Simple Past: 'caught' (V2 of 'catch') → 'was caught' (singular subject 'thief').

examples.text: Active: Workers were repairing the road. / Passive: The road was being repaired by the workers.
examples.note: Past Continuous: 'were repairing' → 'was being repaired' (singular 'road').

examples.text: Active: She had already submitted the form. / Passive: The form had already been submitted by her.
examples.note: Past Perfect: 'had submitted' → 'had been submitted'. Adverb 'already' is retained.

examples.text: Active: They did not invite him. / Passive: He was not invited by them.
examples.note: Simple Past negative: 'did not invite' → 'was not invited'. 'him' (object) → 'he' (new subject).

examples.text: Active: The teacher was explaining the lesson when I arrived. / Passive: The lesson was being explained by the teacher when I arrived.
examples.note: Past Continuous: 'was explaining' → 'was being explained'. The time clause 'when I arrived' is unchanged.

commonMistakes.wrong: The letter were written by him.
commonMistakes.right: The letter was written by him.
commonMistakes.note: 'Letter' is singular; 'was' must be used, not 'were'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The bridge was being build by the workers.
commonMistakes.right: The bridge was being built by the workers.
commonMistakes.note: 'build' is the base form (V1); the past participle (V3) of 'build' is 'built'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The work had been being done by them.
commonMistakes.right: The work had been done by them.
commonMistakes.note: Past Perfect Continuous passive is not standard. Use Past Perfect passive 'had been done'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The documents was stolen.
commonMistakes.right: The documents were stolen.
commonMistakes.note: 'Documents' is plural; 'were' must be used, not 'was'.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'The workers were constructing the dam.'
options: The dam was being constructed by the workers.
The dam was constructed by the workers.
The dam had been constructed by the workers.
The dam is being constructed by the workers.
practice.explanation: Past Continuous passive: 'were constructing' → 'was being constructed'. Singular 'dam' takes 'was'. Option a is correct.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'The jury had announced the verdict before noon.'
options: The verdict was announced before noon by the jury.
The verdict had been announced before noon by the jury.
The verdict had announced before noon by the jury.
The verdict has been announced before noon by the jury.
practice.explanation: Past Perfect passive: 'had announced' → 'had been announced'. The time phrase 'before noon' is retained. Option b is correct.

practice.question: Active: 'She did not complete the task.' Which passive is correct?
options: The task is not completed by her.
The task has not been completed by her.
The task was not completed by her.
The task were not completed by her.
practice.explanation: Simple Past negative: 'did not complete' → 'was not completed'. Singular 'task' takes 'was'. Option c is correct.

quiz.question: Identify the passive tense: 'The letter had been delivered before he arrived.'
quiz.explanation: The structure 'had been + V3' identifies this as Past Perfect Passive.

quiz.question: Active: 'The chef was preparing the meal.' Correct passive: ___
options: The meal was prepared by the chef.
The meal had been prepared by the chef.
The meal was being prepared by the chef.
The meal were being prepared by the chef.
quiz.explanation: Past Continuous: 'was preparing' → 'was being prepared'. Singular 'meal' takes 'was'. Option c is correct.

quiz.question: Which sentence contains a voice conversion error?
options: The books were returned by the students.
The bridge was being built by the engineers.
The report had been submitted by the officer.
The cake were baked by my mother.
quiz.explanation: 'Cake' is singular; 'was' must be used, not 'were'. All other options have correct number agreement.

content.summary: Past tense passive constructions use: Simple Past → was/were + V3; Past Continuous → was/were + being + V3; Past Perfect → had + been + V3. Past Perfect Continuous has no standard passive form. Use 'was' for singular and 'were' for plural new subjects in Simple Past and Past Continuous passives.

content.introduction: The present tenses in English include Simple Present, Present Continuous, and Present Perfect, each with its own passive structure. Present Perfect Continuous is rarely used in passive voice and is generally avoided in formal writing. Knowing the exact passive formula for each present tense is a high-frequency exam requirement.
content.urduExplanation: Present Tenses میں Passive Voice بنانے کے تین اہم طریقے ہیں۔ Simple Present میں 'am/is/are + V3' استعمال ہوتا ہے، جیسے 'She writes letters' → 'Letters are written by her'۔ Present Continuous میں 'am/is/are + being + V3' آتا ہے، جیسے 'He is reading the book' → 'The book is being read by him'۔ Present Perfect میں 'has/have + been + V3' لگتا ہے، جیسے 'They have completed the work' → 'The work has been completed by them'۔ Present Perfect Continuous کا Passive Voice عام طور پر نہیں بنایا جاتا کیونکہ یہ بہت بوجھل ہو جاتا ہے۔
content.englishExplanation: There are three present tenses that regularly form passive voice constructions. Simple Present Passive uses 'am/is/are + V3'. The choice of am/is/are depends on the new subject: singular third-person takes 'is', plural takes 'are', and first-person singular takes 'am'. Formula: Subject + am/is/are + V3 + (by + agent). Present Continuous Passive uses 'am/is/are + being + V3'. The 'being' marker signals the continuous aspect in passive. Formula: Subject + am/is/are + being + V3 + (by + agent). Present Perfect Passive uses 'has/have + been + V3'. 'has' is used with singular third-person subjects; 'have' with plural or first/second-person subjects. Formula: Subject + has/have + been + V3 + (by + agent). Present Perfect Continuous passive ('has/have been being + V3') is grammatically possible but extremely rare and avoided in standard usage.

types.name: Simple Present Passive
types.description: Active: Subject + V1(s/es) + Object → Passive: Object + am/is/are + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'The teacher explains the lesson.' → 'The lesson is explained by the teacher.'

types.name: Present Continuous Passive
types.description: Active: Subject + am/is/are + V1-ing + Object → Passive: Object + am/is/are + being + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'She is writing a report.' → 'A report is being written by her.'

types.name: Present Perfect Passive
types.description: Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object → Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + agent. Example: 'He has finished the assignment.' → 'The assignment has been finished by him.'

types.name: Present Perfect Continuous (Passive – Not Standard)
types.description: Present Perfect Continuous passive is not used in standard English. If you see 'She has been writing the report for two hours', it remains in active or is rephrased.

rules: Simple Present passive: am/is/are + V3. Match the auxiliary to the new subject's number and person.
Present Continuous passive: am/is/are + being + V3. Never omit 'being' in this form.
Present Perfect passive: has/have + been + V3. Use 'has' for singular third-person new subjects; 'have' otherwise.
Present Perfect Continuous does NOT have a standard passive form; avoid it in exams.
The past participle (V3) must be correct — irregular verbs must be memorised (write→written, take→taken, do→done).
Number agreement: singular new subject → is/was/has; plural new subject → are/were/have.
Negative: insert 'not' after the first auxiliary (is not written, are not being reviewed, has not been completed).

examples.text: Active: The government announces new policies every year. / Passive: New policies are announced by the government every year.
examples.note: Simple Present: 'announces' → 'are announced' (plural subject 'new policies').

examples.text: Active: She is teaching the students. / Passive: The students are being taught by her.
examples.note: Present Continuous: 'is teaching' → 'are being taught' (plural 'students'). 'She' → 'her'.

examples.text: Active: He has written three books. / Passive: Three books have been written by him.
examples.note: Present Perfect: 'has written' → 'have been written' (plural subject 'three books').

examples.text: Active: I am not reading this novel. / Passive: This novel is not being read by me.
examples.note: Negative Present Continuous: 'am not reading' → 'is not being read'. 'I' → 'me'.

examples.text: Active: The committee has not yet approved the budget. / Passive: The budget has not yet been approved by the committee.
examples.note: Present Perfect negative: 'has not yet approved' → 'has not yet been approved'. Adverb 'yet' stays.

commonMistakes.wrong: The lesson are explained by the teacher.
commonMistakes.right: The lesson is explained by the teacher.
commonMistakes.note: 'Lesson' is singular; must use 'is', not 'are'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The work is been completed by them.
commonMistakes.right: The work has been completed by them.
commonMistakes.note: Present Perfect passive requires 'has/have been + V3', not 'is been + V3'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The report is being wrote by her.
commonMistakes.right: The report is being written by her.
commonMistakes.note: 'wrote' is simple past, not V3. The correct past participle of 'write' is 'written'.

commonMistakes.wrong: He has been being taught by her for years.
commonMistakes.right: He has been taught by her for years. (Rephrase to Present Perfect passive.)
commonMistakes.note: Present Perfect Continuous passive is not standard. Use Present Perfect passive instead.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'The students are solving the problems.'
options: The problems are being solved by the students.
The problems were being solved by the students.
The problems are solved by the students.
The problems have been solved by the students.
practice.explanation: Present Continuous passive: 'are solving' → 'are being solved'. The object 'problems' (plural) becomes the subject, taking 'are'. Option a is correct.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'She has not completed her homework.'
options: Her homework is not completed by her.
Her homework has not been completed by her.
Her homework was not completed by her.
Her homework had not been completed by her.
practice.explanation: Present Perfect negative: 'has not completed' → 'has not been completed'. Tense stays Present Perfect. Option b is correct.

practice.question: Active: 'People speak French in many countries.' Which passive is correct?
options: French is spoken in many countries.
French is speaking in many countries.
French was spoken in many countries.
French has been speaking in many countries.
practice.explanation: Simple Present passive: 'speak' → 'is spoken'. The agent 'people' is vague and omitted. Option a is correct.

quiz.question: Which is the correct Present Perfect passive of: 'They have destroyed many forests'?
options: Many forests have destroyed by them.
Many forests are destroyed by them.
Many forests have been destroyed by them.
Many forests had been destroyed by them.
quiz.explanation: Present Perfect passive = have/has + been + V3. 'have destroyed' → 'have been destroyed'. Plural subject 'forests' takes 'have'. Option c is correct.

quiz.question: Identify the tense of this passive sentence: 'The application is being processed.'
quiz.explanation: The structure 'is being + V3' is the marker of Present Continuous Passive.

quiz.question: Active: 'I am reading a novel.' Correct passive is ___
options: A novel was read by me.
A novel is being read by me.
A novel has been read by me.
A novel is read by me.
quiz.explanation: Present Continuous: 'am reading' → 'is being read'. 'I' → 'me'. Singular 'novel' takes 'is'. Option b is correct.

content.summary: Present tenses form passive using: Simple Present → am/is/are + V3; Present Continuous → am/is/are + being + V3; Present Perfect → has/have + been + V3. Present Perfect Continuous has no standard passive form and should be avoided. Always match the auxiliary number to the new subject and use the correct past participle (V3).

content.introduction: Converting a sentence from active to passive voice requires following a precise set of rules. These rules cover how to reposition the object, how to change the verb form, how to introduce the agent, and how to adjust pronoun cases correctly. Mastering these rules is essential for competitive exams.
content.urduExplanation: Active سے Passive Voice بنانے کے لیے چند اہم اصول یاد رکھنے ضروری ہیں۔ پہلا اصول: Active کا Object، Passive کا Subject بنتا ہے۔ دوسرا اصول: Verb کی شکل 'be (اسی tense میں) + V3 (past participle)' میں بدل جاتی ہے۔ تیسرا اصول: Active کا Subject، 'by' لگا کر آخر میں آتا ہے، اور اگر وہ Pronoun ہو تو object case استعمال ہوتا ہے (I→me, he→him, she→her, they→them, we→us)۔ چوتھا اصول: صرف Transitive Verbs (وہ افعال جن کا Object ہو) ہی Passive میں بدل سکتے ہیں۔
content.englishExplanation: The general rules of active-to-passive conversion apply across all tenses and sentence types. Rule 1 – Object becomes Subject: The direct object of the active verb moves to the subject position of the passive clause. Rule 2 – Verb changes to 'be + V3': The main verb is replaced by the appropriate form of 'be' (matching the original tense) followed by the past participle. Rule 3 – Subject becomes 'by + agent': The original subject is placed after the verb phrase, preceded by 'by'. If it is a pronoun, it must change to the object case. Rule 4 – Pronoun case changes: I→me, we→us, he→him, she→her, they→them, you and it remain unchanged. Rule 5 – Omit the agent when it is 'someone', 'people', 'they' (vague) or when contextually obvious. Rule 6 – Only transitive verbs can be passivised; intransitive verbs ('go', 'sleep', 'arrive') cannot. Rule 7 – Number agreement: The new subject (old object) determines the number of the 'be' auxiliary.

types.name: Object → Subject
types.description: The direct object of the active sentence is repositioned as the subject of the passive sentence. Example: 'Ali wrote [a letter]' → '[A letter] was written by Ali.'

types.name: Verb → be + V3 (same tense)
types.description: The active main verb is replaced with the appropriate tense of 'be' plus the past participle. Example: 'writes'(Simple Present) → 'is written'; 'wrote'(Simple Past) → 'was written'.

types.name: Subject → by + agent (object pronoun)
types.description: The original subject becomes the agent phrase. Pronouns change case: I→me, he→him, she→her, we→us, they→them. Example: 'She ate it' → 'It was eaten by her.'

types.name: Pronoun Case Conversion Table
types.description: I → me | We → us | He → him | She → her | They → them | You → you | It → it

types.name: Omitting the Agent
types.description: When the agent is vague (someone, people, they) or unknown, the 'by + agent' phrase is dropped. Example: 'Someone stole my bag.' → 'My bag was stolen.'

types.name: Number Agreement of 'be'
types.description: The auxiliary 'be' must agree in number with the new subject (original object). 'The letters were sent.' (plural) vs. 'The letter was sent.' (singular)

rules: Object of active sentence → Subject of passive sentence.
Active verb → appropriate tense of 'be' + past participle (V3).
Subject of active sentence → 'by' + agent (in object pronoun form if a pronoun).
Pronoun changes: I→me, we→us, he→him, she→her, they→them; you, it remain same.
If agent is vague (someone/people/they/everyone) or unknown, omit 'by + agent'.
Only transitive verbs (those taking a direct object) can be converted to passive voice.
The auxiliary 'be' must agree in number and person with the new passive subject.
Negative sentences: place 'not' after the first auxiliary. 'He did not write it.' → 'It was not written by him.'

examples.text: Active: I wrote this letter. / Passive: This letter was written by me.
examples.note: 'I' (subject pronoun) changes to 'me' (object pronoun) after 'by'.

examples.text: Active: They built the bridge. / Passive: The bridge was built (by them).
examples.note: 'They' is a general/vague agent; 'by them' may be omitted. 'built' is V3 of 'build'.

examples.text: Active: He does not trust her. / Passive: She is not trusted by him.
examples.note: Negative retained; 'does not trust' → 'is not trusted'. 'her' (object) becomes 'she' (new subject).

examples.text: Active: The teacher praises the students. / Passive: The students are praised by the teacher.
examples.note: Plural object 'students' → plural subject; 'are' used instead of 'is'.

examples.text: Active: We have completed the project. / Passive: The project has been completed by us.
examples.note: Present Perfect; 'We' → 'us'; 'have completed' → 'has been completed' (new subject is singular).

commonMistakes.wrong: The letter was wrote by I.
commonMistakes.right: The letter was written by me.
commonMistakes.note: Two errors: V3 must be used ('written' not 'wrote'); subject pronoun 'I' → object pronoun 'me' after 'by'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The books is given to him.
commonMistakes.right: The books are given to him.
commonMistakes.note: 'Books' is plural, so the auxiliary must be 'are', not 'is'.

commonMistakes.wrong: She is slept by him.
commonMistakes.right: No passive form — 'sleep' is intransitive.
commonMistakes.note: Intransitive verbs cannot be made passive. 'Sleep' takes no object.

commonMistakes.wrong: The cake was ate by the children.
commonMistakes.right: The cake was eaten by the children.
commonMistakes.note: 'ate' is simple past tense, not the past participle. The correct V3 is 'eaten'.

practice.question: Change to passive: 'She teaches us English.'
options: English is taught to us by her.
English was taught to us by her.
English is taught to we by she.
English is teaching by her to us.
practice.explanation: Simple Present: 'teaches' → 'is taught'. 'us' stays 'us' (object pronoun, unchanged). 'She' → 'her' after 'by'. Correct: 'English is taught to us by her.'

practice.question: Which pronoun correctly completes the passive: 'The report was submitted by ___.'?
practice.explanation: After 'by', use object pronouns. 'he' is a subject pronoun; 'him' is the correct object pronoun form.

practice.question: Active: 'They did not invite her to the party.' Passive: ___
options: She is not invited to the party by them.
She was not invited to the party by they.
Her was not invited to the party by them.
She was not invited to the party by them.
practice.explanation: Simple Present passive: 'speak' → 'is spoken'. The agent 'people' is vague and omitted. Option d is correct.

quiz.question: Active: 'He admires her courage.' Which passive is correct?
options: Her courage is admired by him.
Her courage was admired by him.
His courage is admired by her.
Her courage is admired by he.
quiz.explanation: Simple Present 'admires' → 'is admired'. The object 'her courage' becomes subject. 'He' → 'him' after 'by'. Option a is correct.

quiz.question: Which of the following CANNOT be converted to passive voice?
quiz.explanation: 'Arrive' is an intransitive verb — it has no direct object. Only transitive verbs can form passive constructions.

quiz.question: Active: 'We are painting the wall.' Passive: ___
options: The wall is being painted by us.
The wall was being painted by us.
The wall is painted by us.
The wall has been painted by us.
quiz.explanation: Present Continuous passive: 'am/is/are being + V3'. 'are painting' → 'is being painted'. 'We' → 'us'. Option a is correct.

content.summary: The core rules of active-to-passive conversion are: object becomes subject, verb changes to 'be + V3' in the same tense, and the original subject becomes 'by + agent' (using object pronoun form). The agent is omitted when vague or unknown, and only transitive verbs can be passivised. Number agreement between the new subject and the 'be' auxiliary is mandatory.

content.introduction: Imperative sentences express commands, instructions, or directions. In Direct Speech they begin with a base verb (e.g., 'Sit down.', 'Do not speak.'). Converting them into Indirect Speech involves replacing 'said' with an appropriate reporting verb and using the infinitive form 'to + base verb'. For negative commands, 'not to + base verb' is used. These forms are tested in every major CSS/PMS grammar section.
content.urduExplanation: حکمیہ جملوں (Imperative Sentences) کو Indirect Speech میں بدلتے وقت Reporting Verb کی جگہ حکم کی نوعیت کے مطابق 'ordered', 'commanded', 'told', 'directed', یا 'instructed' استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ Direct Speech کا base verb 'to + verb' (Infinitive) میں تبدیل ہو جاتا ہے، مثلاً 'Go' → 'to go'۔ منفی حکم (Negative Command) میں 'Do not' یا 'Don't' کی جگہ 'not to + verb' آتا ہے، مثلاً 'Don't shout' → 'not to shout'۔ inverted commas اور exclamatory punctuation ہٹا دی جاتی ہے۔ حکمیہ جملوں میں تنسیخ (Tense Back-shift) لاگو نہیں ہوتی کیونکہ Infinitive (to + verb) کا کوئی زمانہ نہیں ہوتا۔
content.englishExplanation: In Indirect Speech, the imperative sentence loses its base-verb-first structure and is converted using a 'to + infinitive' construction. The reporting verb 'said' is replaced by a verb that conveys the tone of the command: 'ordered' or 'commanded' for strong/military commands, 'told' for general instructions, 'directed' or 'instructed' for formal/official orders, 'warned' for cautionary commands, and 'forbade' for prohibitions. The structure becomes: Reporting Verb + Object + (not) to + base verb + rest of sentence. Because an infinitive has no tense, tense back-shift does not apply to imperative conversions. Pronouns and time/place words do change as per the usual rules. If the command begins with 'Let us / Let's', it converts to 'suggested that they should' or 'proposed that they should'. If the command begins with 'Let him/her/them', it converts to 'said that he/she/they should be allowed to'.

types.name: Affirmative command
types.description: Use 'ordered/told/instructed + object + to + base verb': He said to the soldier, 'Stand up.' → He ordered the soldier to stand up.

types.name: Negative command
types.description: Use 'ordered/told + object + not to + base verb': She said, 'Do not make noise.' → She told them not to make noise.

types.name: 'Let us' proposal
types.description: 'Let us/Let's + verb' → 'suggested/proposed that they/we should + verb': He said, 'Let's go.' → He suggested that they should go.

types.name: 'Let him/her/them' permission
types.description: 'Let him/her/them + verb' → 'said that he/she/they should be allowed to + verb': She said, 'Let him speak.' → She said that he should be allowed to speak.

types.name: Reporting verb choice by tone
types.description: Strong/military: 'commanded/ordered'; general: 'told'; formal/official: 'instructed/directed'; caution: 'warned'; prohibition: 'forbade + from + gerund'.

rules: Replace 'said' with the appropriate reporting verb: ordered, commanded, told, instructed, directed, warned, or forbade depending on the tone.
For affirmative commands: use Reporting Verb + Object + to + base verb.
For negative commands: use Reporting Verb + Object + not to + base verb (do not write 'to not').
Tense back-shift does NOT apply because the infinitive 'to + verb' has no tense.
Pronouns still change according to the SOC rule.
Time and place words (now→then, here→there, today→that day) still change where relevant.
For 'Let us/Let's' commands, use 'suggested/proposed that they/we should + base verb'.
For 'Let him/her/them' commands, use 'said that he/she/they should be allowed to + base verb'.

examples.text: Direct: The general said to the soldiers, 'Attack the enemy.' / Indirect: The general ordered the soldiers to attack the enemy.
examples.note: 'said to' → 'ordered'; affirmative command → 'to attack'; no tense back-shift needed.

examples.text: Direct: The teacher said to the students, 'Do not talk in class.' / Indirect: The teacher told the students not to talk in class.
examples.note: Negative command; 'Do not' → 'not to'; 'said to' → 'told'.

examples.text: Direct: The doctor said to the patient, 'Take this medicine twice a day.' / Indirect: The doctor instructed the patient to take that medicine twice a day.
examples.note: Formal/medical context → 'instructed'; 'this' → 'that'.

examples.text: Direct: He said, 'Let's start the meeting.' / Indirect: He suggested that they should start the meeting.
examples.note: 'Let's' → 'suggested that they should'; first-person plural changes from 'us' to 'they'.

examples.text: Direct: She said to him, 'Don't ever lie to me again.' / Indirect: She warned him never to lie to her again.
examples.note: Cautionary negative → 'warned'; 'Don't ever' → 'never to'; 'me' → 'her'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The teacher told the students to not talk in class.
commonMistakes.right: The teacher told the students not to talk in class.
commonMistakes.note: In British English (standard for CSS/PMS), 'not to' (split infinitive avoidance) is preferred over 'to not'.

commonMistakes.wrong: He ordered the soldiers that they should attack.
commonMistakes.right: He ordered the soldiers to attack.
commonMistakes.note: Commands use 'to + base verb' infinitive construction, not 'that + should' (that form is used for 'let us' suggestions).

commonMistakes.wrong: She said to me to come here now.
commonMistakes.right: She told me to come there then.
commonMistakes.note: 'said to me' → 'told me'; 'here' → 'there'; 'now' → 'then' — place and time words must be changed.

commonMistakes.wrong: He suggested that they go.
commonMistakes.right: He suggested that they should go.
commonMistakes.note: When converting 'Let's', the modal 'should' is required in the reported clause: 'suggested that + subject + should + verb'.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: The officer said to the clerk, 'Submit the report immediately.'
options: The officer ordered the clerk to submit the report immediately.
The officer told the clerk that he should submit the report immediately.
The officer said the clerk to submit the report immediately.
The officer commanded the clerk that submit the report.
practice.explanation: 'said to' → 'ordered' (authoritative command); affirmative command → 'to submit'; infinitive construction used.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: She said to him, 'Do not enter this room.'
options: She told him to not enter that room.
She told him not to enter that room.
She said him not to enter this room.
She ordered him that he should not enter that room.
practice.explanation: 'said to him' → 'told him'; negative command → 'not to enter'; 'this' → 'that'; 'not to' preferred over 'to not'.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: He said, 'Let's complete the project today.'
options: He told them to complete the project today.
He said that they complete the project that day.
He suggested that they should complete the project that day.
He proposed to complete the project today.
practice.explanation: 'Let's' → 'suggested that they should'; 'today' → 'that day'; the full structure is: suggested + that + subject + should + verb.

quiz.question: Which reporting verb is most appropriate for a strong military command in Indirect Speech?
quiz.explanation: 'Ordered' or 'commanded' conveys the strong, authoritative tone of a military command. 'Told' is used for general instructions.

quiz.question: The negative command 'Do not enter' changes to which form in Indirect Speech?
quiz.explanation: Negative commands use 'not to + base verb'. 'To not enter' is an informal split infinitive avoided in formal/exam writing.

quiz.question: 'He said, Let us begin.' The correct Indirect Speech is:
options: He said that they should begin.
He suggested that they should begin.
quiz.explanation: 'Let us/Let's + verb' converts to 'suggested/proposed that + subject + should + verb'. 'Suggested' is the standard reporting verb for proposals.

content.summary: To convert imperative sentences: choose a reporting verb matching the tone (ordered, told, instructed, warned, suggested); use 'to + base verb' for affirmative commands and 'not to + base verb' for negative commands; tense back-shift does not apply because infinitives have no tense; change pronouns and time/place words as usual; and convert 'Let us' to 'suggested that they should + verb'.

content.introduction: Exclamatory sentences express strong emotions: joy, sorrow, surprise, wonder, anger, or disgust. They are introduced by interjections (Hurrah!, Alas!, Bravo!, Oh!, Wow!, What a!, How!) and end with an exclamation mark. In Indirect Speech, the emotion is expressed through an adverbial phrase attached to the reporting verb, the interjection is dropped, and the exclamation mark is removed. These conversions are popular in CSS/PMS objective grammar sections.
content.urduExplanation: جذباتی جملوں (Exclamatory Sentences) میں خوشی، غم، حیرت، یا تعریف کا اظہار ہوتا ہے اور یہ 'Hurrah!', 'Alas!', 'Bravo!', 'What a!', 'How!' جیسے الفاظ سے شروع ہوتے ہیں۔ Indirect Speech میں Reporting Verb کے ساتھ جذبے کا وصف لگاتے ہیں: 'exclaimed with joy' (خوشی)، 'exclaimed with sorrow/grief' (غم)، 'exclaimed with surprise/wonder' (حیرت)، 'exclaimed with admiration' (تعریف)۔ Interjection (Hurrah، Alas وغیرہ) حذف ہو جاتا ہے اور exclamation mark (!) ہٹا دی جاتی ہے۔ جملے کو 'that' کے ذریعے بیانیہ جملے میں بدلتے ہیں اور بقیہ تمام اصول (tense back-shift، ضمیر، وقت کے الفاظ) لاگو ہوتے ہیں۔ 'What a + noun' اور 'How + adjective' والے exclamatory جملے Indirect میں ایک بیانیہ جملے کی صورت اختیار کر لیتے ہیں۔
content.englishExplanation: When converting exclamatory sentences to Indirect Speech, the reporting verb changes from 'said' to 'exclaimed' accompanied by an adverb phrase that captures the emotion: 'exclaimed with joy' (Hurrah, Bravo, Hurray), 'exclaimed with sorrow/grief' (Alas, Oh dear), 'exclaimed with surprise/wonder' (Oh!, What!, How unexpected), 'exclaimed with admiration' (What a lovely/beautiful...), 'exclaimed with disgust' (Ugh!, Fie!), and 'exclaimed with anger' (How dare you!).The interjection itself (Hurrah, Alas, Bravo, Oh, Wow) is omitted completely. The exclamation mark is replaced with a full stop. The conjunction 'that' is inserted after 'exclaimed with [emotion]'. The exclamatory structure 'What a + adjective + noun!' or 'How + adjective!' is rewritten as an assertive clause: 'What a beautiful scene!' → 'exclaimed with admiration that it was a very beautiful scene.' All tense back-shift, pronoun, and time/place word rules apply as normal.

types.name: Joy / Happiness (Hurrah!, Hurray!, Bravo!)
types.description: Reporting phrase: 'exclaimed with joy that': He said, 'Hurrah! We have won.' → He exclaimed with joy that they had won.

types.name: Sorrow / Grief (Alas!, Oh dear!, What a pity!)
types.description: Reporting phrase: 'exclaimed with sorrow that': She said, 'Alas! I have lost everything.' → She exclaimed with sorrow that she had lost everything.

types.name: Surprise / Wonder (Oh!, What!, How!)
types.description: Reporting phrase: 'exclaimed with surprise that': He said, 'Oh! What a strange coincidence!' → He exclaimed with surprise that it was a very strange coincidence.

types.name: Admiration / Praise (What a lovely...!, How beautiful...!)
types.description: Reporting phrase: 'exclaimed with admiration that': She said, 'What a beautiful painting!' → She exclaimed with admiration that it was a very beautiful painting.

types.name: Disgust / Anger (Ugh!, Fie!, How dare you!)
types.description: Reporting phrase: 'exclaimed with disgust/anger that': He said, 'Ugh! How disgusting this is!' → He exclaimed with disgust that it was very disgusting.

rules: Change the reporting verb from 'said' to 'exclaimed' with an appropriate emotion adverb (with joy, with sorrow, with surprise, with admiration, with disgust).
Omit the interjection (Hurrah, Alas, Bravo, Oh, Wow, Ugh) entirely — do not transfer it to Indirect Speech.
Remove the exclamation mark (!) and replace with a full stop.
Insert the conjunction 'that' after the reporting phrase ('exclaimed with joy that...').
Convert exclamatory structures 'What a + adj + noun!' or 'How + adj/adv!' into an assertive clause using 'very': 'What a brave soldier!' → 'that he was a very brave soldier'.
Apply all tense back-shift rules (present→past, present perfect→past perfect, etc.).
Apply pronoun changes (SOC rule) and time/place word changes (now→then, here→there, etc.).
If the emotion is unclear from the interjection, infer from context; when in doubt, 'exclaimed with surprise' is a safe choice for general exclamations.

examples.text: Direct: He said, 'Hurrah! We have won the match.' / Indirect: He exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
examples.note: 'Hurrah' → 'exclaimed with joy'; 'We' → 'they'; 'have won' → 'had won' (present perfect → past perfect).

examples.text: Direct: She said, 'Alas! My brother has failed.' / Indirect: She exclaimed with sorrow that her brother had failed.
examples.note: 'Alas' → 'exclaimed with sorrow'; 'My' → 'her'; 'has failed' → 'had failed'.

examples.text: Direct: He said, 'What a beautiful scene this is!' / Indirect: He exclaimed with admiration that it was a very beautiful scene.
examples.note: 'What a beautiful scene!' → assertive 'it was a very beautiful scene'; exclamatory structure dissolved.

examples.text: Direct: She said, 'How clever you are!' / Indirect: She exclaimed with admiration that I was very clever.
examples.note: 'How + adjective + you are!' → 'very clever'; 'you' → 'I' (reporter is 'me' = object of her exclamation).

examples.text: Direct: The crowd said, 'Bravo! The player has scored a century.' / Indirect: The crowd exclaimed with joy that the player had scored a century.
examples.note: 'Bravo' → 'exclaimed with joy'; third person 'the player' unchanged; 'has scored' → 'had scored'.

commonMistakes.wrong: He exclaimed with joy 'Hurrah!' that they had won.
commonMistakes.right: He exclaimed with joy that they had won.
commonMistakes.note: The interjection 'Hurrah' must be removed entirely, not placed within the indirect clause.

commonMistakes.wrong: She said with sorrow that her brother had failed.
commonMistakes.right: She exclaimed with sorrow that her brother had failed.
commonMistakes.note: The reporting verb must change from 'said' to 'exclaimed'. 'Said with sorrow' is grammatically odd; 'exclaimed with sorrow' is the standard form.

commonMistakes.wrong: He exclaimed with admiration that what a beautiful scene it was.
commonMistakes.right: He exclaimed with admiration that it was a very beautiful scene.
commonMistakes.note: 'What a...' exclamatory structure must be converted to an assertive clause using 'very'; the exclamatory form cannot be retained in Indirect Speech.

commonMistakes.wrong: She exclaimed with admiration that you are very clever.
commonMistakes.right: She exclaimed with admiration that I was very clever.
commonMistakes.note: 'you' → 'I' (object rule, as 'she' exclaimed about the listener); 'are' → 'was' (tense back-shift).

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: She said, 'Hurray! We have passed the exam.'
options: She exclaimed with joy that they had passed the exam.
She said with joy that we have passed the exam.
She exclaimed with joy that we had passed the exam.
She exclaimed joyfully that they have passed the exam.
practice.explanation: 'Hurray' → 'exclaimed with joy'; 'We' → 'they' (third person, since the reporter is separate); 'have passed' → 'had passed' (back-shift).

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: He said, 'Alas! I have lost my wallet.'
options: He exclaimed with surprise that he had lost his wallet.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he had lost his wallet.
He said with sorrow that he has lost his wallet.
He exclaimed with grief that he lost his wallet.
practice.explanation: 'Alas' signals sorrow → 'exclaimed with sorrow'; 'I' → 'he'; 'my' → 'his'; 'have lost' → 'had lost' (present perfect → past perfect).

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: She said, 'What a wonderful gift this is!'
options: She exclaimed with admiration that what a wonderful gift it was.
She exclaimed with surprise that it was a wonderful gift.
She exclaimed with admiration that it was a very wonderful gift.
She exclaimed that it was a very wonderful gift.
practice.explanation: 'What a + adj + noun!' → 'exclaimed with admiration that it was a very + adj + noun'; 'this' → 'it'; tense back-shifts: 'is' → 'was'.

quiz.question: Which reporting phrase replaces 'Alas!' in Indirect Speech?
quiz.explanation: 'Alas' expresses sorrow or grief. Its Indirect Speech equivalent is 'exclaimed with sorrow that' or 'exclaimed with grief that'.

quiz.question: How is 'What a brave soldier he is!' converted to Indirect Speech?
options: He exclaimed that what a brave soldier he was.
He exclaimed with admiration that he was a very brave soldier.
He exclaimed with admiration that what a brave soldier he was.
He exclaimed with admiration that he was a brave soldier.
quiz.explanation: 'What a + adjective + noun!' converts to an assertive clause: 'he was a very brave soldier'. 'Very' replaces the exclamatory structure. 'Exclaimed with admiration' for praise.

quiz.question: What happens to the exclamation mark (!) in Indirect Speech?
options: It is kept at the end of the sentence.
It is moved after the reporting verb.
It is replaced with a full stop.
It is replaced with a question mark.
quiz.explanation: The exclamation mark is always removed in Indirect Speech and replaced with a full stop, since the reported sentence becomes assertive.

content.summary: To convert exclamatory sentences: change 'said' to 'exclaimed with [emotion]' (joy, sorrow, surprise, admiration, disgust); omit the interjection entirely; remove the exclamation mark; insert 'that'; convert 'What a...!' and 'How...!' structures to assertive clauses using 'very'; and apply all tense, pronoun, and time/place word changes as normal.

content.introduction: Converting interrogative (question) sentences into Indirect Speech requires special rules beyond those used for statements. There are two categories: Yes/No questions (answered with yes or no) and Wh-questions (beginning with who, what, where, when, why, how, which). Both types use 'asked' or 'enquired' as the reporting verb, and the question mark is always dropped. These rules are frequently tested in CSS/PMS grammar papers and IELTS.
content.urduExplanation: سوالیہ جملوں (Interrogative Sentences) کو Indirect Speech میں بدلتے وقت Reporting Verb 'said' کی جگہ 'asked' یا 'enquired' استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ ہاں/نہیں والے سوالوں (Yes/No Questions) میں inverted commas کی جگہ 'if' یا 'whether' لگاتے ہیں اور جملے کی ترتیب عام بیانیہ جملے جیسی ہو جاتی ہے۔ Wh-Questions میں وہی wh-word conjunction کا کام کرتا ہے — الگ conjunction کی ضرورت نہیں ہوتی۔ دونوں صورتوں میں Helping Verb (do/does/did) ختم ہو جاتی ہے اور Subject پہلے آتا ہے، Verb بعد میں (Statement Order)۔ Question Mark (؟) بھی ہٹا دیتے ہیں اور زمانہ، ضمائر اور وقت کے الفاظ وہی اصولوں کے مطابق بدلتے ہیں جو بیانیہ جملوں میں لاگو ہوتے ہیں۔
content.englishExplanation: When converting an interrogative sentence to Indirect Speech, the reporting verb changes from 'said' to 'asked' (or 'enquired', 'wanted to know', 'wondered'). The question mark is removed and the sentence is restructured into affirmative (statement) word order: Subject + Verb + Object/Complement — the inverted question-word order (Auxiliary + Subject + Verb) is abandoned. Auxiliary verbs do/does/did used only for question formation are dropped; any information they carry is expressed through the back-shifted main verb. For Yes/No questions, the conjunction 'if' or 'whether' is inserted after the reporting verb. For Wh-questions, the wh-word itself (what, where, when, why, who, how, which) serves as the conjunction — no additional conjunction is needed. All tense back-shift, pronoun, and time/place word changes apply exactly as in assertive sentences. A very common CSS exam trap: students keep 'if' for wh-questions or keep inverted word order — both are wrong.

types.name: Yes/No Question
types.description: Use 'if' or 'whether' as conjunction; drop the question mark; invert to statement order (subject before verb); drop auxiliary do/does/did.

types.name: Wh-Question
types.description: The wh-word (what, where, when, why, who, how, which) itself acts as the conjunction; no extra 'if/whether' is added; statement word order applies.

types.name: Reporting verb change
types.description: 'Said' → 'asked', 'enquired', 'wanted to know', or 'wondered'; if an object is named (e.g., 'said to me'), it becomes 'asked me'.

types.name: Tense back-shift in questions
types.description: Same back-shift rules as assertive sentences apply: present→past, will→would, can→could, etc.

types.name: Pronoun and time-word change
types.description: Same SOC pronoun rule and time/place word substitution (now→then, today→that day, here→there) as in statements.

rules: Change the reporting verb 'said' to 'asked' / 'enquired' / 'wanted to know'; if 'say to + object' was used, write 'asked + object'.
Remove the question mark and replace the inverted commas with the appropriate conjunction.
For Yes/No questions: insert 'if' or 'whether' as the conjunction.
For Wh-questions: use the wh-word itself as the conjunction; do not add 'if' or 'whether'.
Change the word order from question order (Auxiliary + Subject + Verb) to statement order (Subject + Verb).
Drop the auxiliary do/does/did that was used purely for forming the question; back-shift the main verb instead.
Apply all tense back-shift rules (present→past, past→past perfect, will→would, can→could, may→might).
Apply pronoun (SOC rule) and time/place word changes (now→then, today→that day, yesterday→the previous day, here→there, this→that).

examples.text: Direct: She said, 'Where do you live?' / Indirect: She asked where I lived.
examples.note: 'do you live' → statement order 'I lived'; wh-word 'where' is conjunction; 'do' dropped; 'you' → 'I' (object of reporting verb 'she asked').

examples.text: Direct: He said to her, 'Are you coming to the party?' / Indirect: He asked her if she was coming to the party.
examples.note: Yes/No question → conjunction 'if'; 'say to her' → 'asked her'; 'you' → 'she'; 'are coming' → 'was coming'.

examples.text: Direct: The officer said to the candidate, 'Why did you apply late?' / Indirect: The officer asked the candidate why he had applied late.
examples.note: Wh-word 'why' is conjunction; 'did you apply' → 'he had applied' (past→past perfect; 'did' dropped).

examples.text: Direct: She said, 'Can you help me now?' / Indirect: She asked if I could help her then.
examples.note: Yes/No → 'if'; 'can' → 'could'; 'you' → 'I' (object rule); 'me' → 'her'; 'now' → 'then'.

examples.text: Direct: The teacher said to the students, 'Have you finished your assignment?' / Indirect: The teacher asked the students if they had finished their assignment.
examples.note: Yes/No → 'if'; 'say to the students' → 'asked the students'; 'you' → 'they'; 'have finished' → 'had finished'; 'your' → 'their'.

commonMistakes.wrong: She asked where did I live.
commonMistakes.right: She asked where I lived.
commonMistakes.note: Question word order (did + subject + verb) must change to statement order (subject + verb) in indirect speech. 'Did' is dropped.

commonMistakes.wrong: He asked her if why she was crying.
commonMistakes.right: He asked her why she was crying.
commonMistakes.note: For Wh-questions, 'if/whether' must NOT be added alongside the wh-word. The wh-word alone is the conjunction.

commonMistakes.wrong: He asked to her where she lived.
commonMistakes.right: He asked her where she lived.
commonMistakes.note: 'Ask' does not take 'to' before its object. It is 'asked + object' not 'asked to + object'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The teacher asked the students if they have finished their assignment.
commonMistakes.right: The teacher asked the students if they had finished their assignment.
commonMistakes.note: Back-shift must be applied: 'have finished' (present perfect) → 'had finished' (past perfect).

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: He said to me, 'Do you know the answer?'
options: He asked me if I knew the answer.
He asked me if you know the answer.
He asked me whether did I know the answer.
He said me if I know the answer.
practice.explanation: 'Say to me' → 'asked me'; Yes/No → 'if'; 'you' → 'I' (object rule); 'do you know' → statement order 'I knew' (present→past); 'do' dropped.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: She said to him, 'When will you return?'
options: She asked him when will he return.
She asked him when he would return.
She asked him if he would return.
She enquired him that when he would return.
practice.explanation: Wh-word 'when' is conjunction (no 'if'); 'say to him' → 'asked him'; 'you' → 'he'; 'will return' → 'would return'; statement order.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: The interviewer said, 'Why have you chosen this field?'
options: The interviewer asked if he had chosen this field.
The interviewer asked that why he had chosen that field.
The interviewer asked why he had chosen that field.
The interviewer asked why has he chosen that field.
practice.explanation: Wh-word 'why' serves as conjunction alone — no 'that' or 'if' needed; 'you' → 'he'; 'have chosen' → 'had chosen'; 'this' → 'that'; statement order.

quiz.question: Which conjunction is used in Indirect Speech for Yes/No questions?
quiz.explanation: Yes/No questions use 'if' or 'whether' as the conjunction. Wh-questions use the wh-word itself.

quiz.question: The teacher said to me, 'Do you understand the lesson?' The correct Indirect Speech is:
options: The teacher asked me that I understood the lesson.
The teacher asked me if I understood the lesson.
The teacher said to me if I understood the lesson.
The teacher asked me whether do I understand the lesson.
quiz.explanation: 'Say to me' → 'asked me'; Yes/No → 'if'; 'you' → 'I'; 'do you understand' → statement order 'I understood'; 'do' dropped.

quiz.question: What word order is used in the reported clause of an indirect question?
quiz.explanation: Indirect questions always use statement (affirmative) word order: Subject + Verb. Question word order is never retained.

content.summary: To convert interrogative sentences: change 'said' to 'asked/enquired'; for Yes/No questions use 'if/whether' as conjunction; for Wh-questions use the wh-word itself as conjunction (never add 'if' alongside it); always switch to statement word order (Subject + Verb) and drop the auxiliary do/does/did; remove the question mark; and apply all standard tense, pronoun, and time/place word changes.

content.introduction: Requests are polite imperatives — the speaker asks someone to do something rather than ordering. They typically contain the word 'please', or begin with 'Could you', 'Would you', 'Will you', 'Can you', or 'Would you mind'. In Indirect Speech, requests use 'requested' or 'asked' as the reporting verb and retain the infinitive 'to + base verb' structure. Distinguishing requests from commands (and choosing the correct reporting verb) is a recurring CSS/PMS exam question.
content.urduExplanation: درخواستی جملوں (Requests) میں عام طور پر 'please' کا لفظ آتا ہے یا 'Could you', 'Would you' جیسے شائستہ فعل استعمال ہوتے ہیں۔ Indirect Speech میں Reporting Verb کے طور پر 'requested' یا 'asked' استعمال ہوتا ہے — حکم والا 'ordered' یا 'commanded' نہیں۔ 'please' ہٹا دیتے ہیں اور فعل کو 'to + base verb' میں بدل دیتے ہیں، جیسے 'Please help me' → 'requested me to help her'۔ اگر درخواست 'Could you' یا 'Would you' سے شروع ہو تو وہ Yes/No سوال کی طرح نہیں بلکہ درخواست کی طرح Indirect ہوتی ہے۔ ضمائر اور وقت کے الفاظ بدلتے ہیں جبکہ tense back-shift infinitive پر لاگو نہیں ہوتی۔
content.englishExplanation: Requests, though grammatically interrogative or imperative in Direct Speech, are treated as a distinct category in Indirect Speech narration. The reporting verb is 'requested' (most formal) or 'asked' (general), never 'ordered' or 'commanded'. The word 'please' is always omitted in Indirect Speech — its politeness is implied by the reporting verb 'requested'. The structure is: Subject + requested/asked + Object + to + base verb + rest. When the request is phrased as a polite question ('Could you please...', 'Would you kindly...'), it still converts to the request structure (not the yes/no question structure), because the pragmatic function is a request, not a genuine question. Tense back-shift does not apply to the infinitive since it is tenseless; however, other changes (pronouns, time/place words) still apply. Negative requests ('Please do not disturb me') convert to 'requested + object + not to + base verb'.

types.name: Request with 'please' (imperative form)
types.description: Drop 'please'; use 'requested + object + to + base verb': She said, 'Please open the window.' → She requested him to open the window.

types.name: Polite question as request ('Could/Would you')
types.description: Treat as a request, not a yes/no question: He said, 'Could you please bring some water?' → He requested her to bring some water.

types.name: Negative request
types.description: Use 'requested/asked + object + not to + base verb': She said, 'Please do not disturb me.' → She requested him not to disturb her.

types.name: 'Would you mind + gerund' form
types.description: Converts to 'requested + object + to + base verb': He said, 'Would you mind closing the door?' → He requested her to close the door.

types.name: Self-directed request ('please let me')
types.description: She said, 'Please let me go.' → She requested him to let her go / She requested to be allowed to go.

rules: Use 'requested' or 'asked' as the reporting verb — never 'ordered' or 'commanded' for polite requests.
Remove the word 'please' entirely — it is not transferred to Indirect Speech.
For affirmative requests: Reporting Verb + Object + to + base verb.
For negative requests: Reporting Verb + Object + not to + base verb.
Polite interrogative requests ('Could you', 'Would you', 'Will you', 'Would you mind') convert using the request structure, not the question (if/whether) structure.
For 'Would you mind + gerund', the gerund changes to a to-infinitive in Indirect Speech.
Tense back-shift does not apply to the infinitive (to + verb), but pronoun and time/place changes still apply.
Use 'asked' when the request is less formal; use 'requested' when it is formal or involves a plea.

examples.text: Direct: She said to him, 'Please help me.' / Indirect: She requested him to help her.
examples.note: 'please' dropped; 'said to him' → 'requested him'; 'me' → 'her'; to-infinitive 'to help'.

examples.text: Direct: He said to the waiter, 'Could you please bring the menu?' / Indirect: He requested the waiter to bring the menu.
examples.note: Polite question treated as request; 'Could you please' → request structure; 'bring' (base verb) stays as 'to bring'.

examples.text: Direct: She said to me, 'Please do not make noise here.' / Indirect: She requested me not to make noise there.
examples.note: Negative request → 'not to make'; 'please' dropped; 'here' → 'there'.

examples.text: Direct: The student said to the teacher, 'Would you please explain this again?' / Indirect: The student requested the teacher to explain that again.
examples.note: Polite interrogative → request form; 'this' → 'that'; 'to explain' used.

examples.text: Direct: She said, 'Would you mind lending me your pen?' / Indirect: She requested him to lend her his pen.
examples.note: 'Would you mind + gerund' → 'requested + object + to + base verb'; gerund 'lending' → infinitive 'to lend'; 'me' → 'her'; 'your' → 'his'.

commonMistakes.wrong: She requested him to please help her.
commonMistakes.right: She requested him to help her.
commonMistakes.note: 'Please' is always omitted in Indirect Speech. Its meaning is already carried by 'requested'.

commonMistakes.wrong: He asked the waiter if he could bring the menu.
commonMistakes.right: He requested the waiter to bring the menu.
commonMistakes.note: A polite request ('Could you bring...') should be converted using the request infinitive structure, not the yes/no question (if/whether) structure.

commonMistakes.wrong: She requested me not make noise.
commonMistakes.right: She requested me not to make noise.
commonMistakes.note: The infinitive marker 'to' must be present even in the negative form: 'not to + base verb', not 'not + base verb'.

commonMistakes.wrong: The student requested the teacher that he explain that again.
commonMistakes.right: The student requested the teacher to explain that again.
commonMistakes.note: Requests do not use a 'that' clause; the correct structure is 'requested + object + to + base verb'.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: She said to me, 'Please lend me your book.'
options: She requested me to lend her my book.
She requested me to please lend her my book.
She asked me if I would lend her my book.
She told me to lend her my book.
practice.explanation: 'said to me' → 'requested me'; 'please' dropped; 'lend me your book' → 'to lend her my book' (me→her, your→my using object rule for pronouns).

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: He said to her, 'Would you mind posting this letter?'
options: He asked her if she would post that letter.
He requested her to post that letter.
He asked her whether she minded posting that letter.
He told her to post this letter.
practice.explanation: 'Would you mind + gerund' → 'requested + object + to + base verb'; gerund 'posting' → 'to post'; 'this' → 'that'; request structure, not question.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: The patient said to the nurse, 'Please do not disturb me now.'
options: The patient requested the nurse not to disturb him then.
The patient asked the nurse to not disturb him now.
The patient requested the nurse please not to disturb him then.
The patient told the nurse not to disturb him then.
practice.explanation: Negative request → 'not to disturb'; 'please' dropped; 'said to the nurse' → 'requested the nurse'; 'me' → 'him'; 'now' → 'then'.

quiz.question: Which reporting verb is most appropriate for converting a polite request?
quiz.explanation: 'Requested' or 'asked' is used for polite requests. 'Ordered' and 'commanded' imply authority, 'told' implies instruction, not politeness.

quiz.question: How is 'please' handled when converting a request to Indirect Speech?
options: It is kept before the infinitive.
quiz.explanation: 'Please' is always omitted in Indirect Speech. The polite tone is conveyed by the reporting verb 'requested' itself.

quiz.question: 'Could you please close the door?' in Indirect Speech becomes:
options: He asked if I could close the door.
He asked whether could I close the door.
He requested me to close the door.
He requested me to please close the door.
quiz.explanation: A polite interrogative request converts to the request infinitive structure (requested + object + to + verb), not a yes/no question. 'Please' is dropped.

content.summary: Requests in Indirect Speech use 'requested' or 'asked' as the reporting verb; 'please' is always omitted. Affirmative requests use 'to + base verb' and negative requests use 'not to + base verb'. Polite interrogative forms like 'Could you / Would you mind' convert to the request (infinitive) structure, not the question (if/whether) structure. Tense back-shift does not apply to the infinitive, but pronoun and time/place word changes always apply.

content.introduction: Narration is the art of reporting what someone has said, either in the speaker's exact words (Direct Speech) or in the reporter's own words (Indirect Speech). Assertive or declarative sentences — statements of fact, opinion, or information — are the most common type converted in CSS, PMS, and IELTS writing tasks. Mastering the systematic rules of tense back-shift, pronoun change, and time/place-word substitution is essential for full marks.
content.urduExplanation: براہِ راست تقریر (Direct Speech) میں ہم کسی کے الفاظ جوں کے توں نقل کرتے ہیں، جبکہ بالواسطہ تقریر (Indirect Speech) میں ہم انہیں اپنے الفاظ میں بیان کرتے ہیں۔ بیانیہ جملوں (Assertive Sentences) میں Reporting Verb 'say' یا 'said' ہو تو اسے 'said' رہنے دیتے ہیں، لیکن اگر Object موجود ہو تو 'told' استعمال کرتے ہیں۔ Inverted commas ہٹا کر Conjunction 'that' لگاتے ہیں — اگرچہ 'that' حذف بھی ہو سکتا ہے۔ Reported Clause کے فعل کا زمانہ ایک قدم پیچھے کرتے ہیں: Present Simple → Past Simple، Present Continuous → Past Continuous، وغیرہ۔ ضمائر (Pronouns) اور وقت و مقام کے الفاظ بھی بدل جاتے ہیں، مثلاً 'now' → 'then'، 'today' → 'that day'، 'here' → 'there'۔
content.englishExplanation: When converting an assertive (declarative) sentence from Direct to Indirect Speech, the reporting verb 'say' becomes 'say' when the subject remains the same, but if an object is present, 'say to' changes to 'tell/told'. The inverted commas are removed and the conjunction 'that' is inserted (though it may be omitted in informal usage). The tense of the reported clause must be back-shifted: Simple Present → Simple Past, Present Continuous → Past Continuous, Simple Past → Past Perfect, Present Perfect → Past Perfect, and Future (will) → Conditional (would). First and second-person pronouns change according to the subject or object of the reporting verb (the SOC rule: Subject, Object, Context). Time and place adverbials also shift: 'now' → 'then', 'today' → 'that day', 'yesterday' → 'the previous day / the day before', 'tomorrow' → 'the next day / the following day', 'here' → 'there', 'this' → 'that', 'these' → 'those'. If the reporting verb is in the present or future tense, tense back-shift does NOT apply.

types.name: say / say that (no object)
types.description: When there is no indirect object, 'said' remains 'said' and 'that' is inserted: He said, 'I am tired.' → He said that he was tired.

types.name: say to → tell / told (with object)
types.description: When 'say to + object' is used, it changes to 'tell/told + object': She said to me, 'You are right.' → She told me that I was right.

types.name: Tense back-shift
types.description: All tenses in the reported clause shift one step back: Simple Present → Simple Past, Past Simple → Past Perfect, will → would, can → could, may → might, must → had to / must.

types.name: Pronoun change (SOC rule)
types.description: First-person pronouns (I/me/my/we/us/our) change according to the Subject of the reporting verb; second-person pronouns (you/your) change according to the Object; third-person pronouns remain unchanged.

types.name: Time and place word change
types.description: Deictic expressions shift to match the new context: now→then, today→that day, yesterday→the previous day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there, this→that, these→those, ago→before.

rules: Remove the inverted commas (quotation marks) and insert the conjunction 'that' after the reporting verb.
Change 'say to + object' to 'tell/told + object'; keep 'said' if there is no object.
Back-shift the tense of the reported verb one step into the past (unless the reporting verb is present/future tense).
Change first-person pronouns according to the subject of the reporting verb (SOC: Subject rule).
Change second-person pronouns according to the object of the reporting verb (SOC: Object rule).
Third-person pronouns (he, she, they, it) remain unchanged.
Replace time/place words: now→then, today→that day, yesterday→the previous day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there, this→that, ago→before.
Do NOT back-shift if the reported clause states a universal truth, habitual fact, or if the reporting verb is in the present/future tense.

examples.text: Direct: He said, 'I am busy.' / Indirect: He said that he was busy.
examples.note: 'I' → 'he' (subject rule); 'am' → 'was' (present→past back-shift); 'said' retained (no object).

examples.text: Direct: She said to me, 'You have done well.' / Indirect: She told me that I had done well.
examples.note: 'say to me' → 'told me'; 'you' → 'I' (object rule); present perfect 'have done' → past perfect 'had done'.

examples.text: Direct: They said, 'We will leave tomorrow.' / Indirect: They said that they would leave the next day.
examples.note: 'We' → 'they'; 'will' → 'would'; 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'.

examples.text: Direct: Ali said to his friend, 'I saw you here yesterday.' / Indirect: Ali told his friend that he had seen him there the previous day.
examples.note: 'saw' → 'had seen'; 'you' → 'him'; 'here' → 'there'; 'yesterday' → 'the previous day'.

examples.text: Direct: The student said, 'I can solve this problem now.' / Indirect: The student said that he could solve that problem then.
examples.note: 'can' → 'could'; 'this' → 'that'; 'now' → 'then'; 'I' → 'he'.

commonMistakes.wrong: She said to me that you are right.
commonMistakes.right: She told me that I was right.
commonMistakes.note: 'say to + object' must become 'tell + object'; 'you' changes to 'I' (object rule); 'are' back-shifts to 'was'.

commonMistakes.wrong: He said that he is tired.
commonMistakes.right: He said that he was tired.
commonMistakes.note: Tense must back-shift: Simple Present 'is' → Simple Past 'was' when the reporting verb is in the past tense.

commonMistakes.wrong: They said that they will come tomorrow.
commonMistakes.right: They said that they would come the next day.
commonMistakes.note: 'will' → 'would' (future → conditional); 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'.

commonMistakes.wrong: She told that she was happy.
commonMistakes.right: She said that she was happy. / She told me that she was happy.
commonMistakes.note: 'Tell' always requires an object ('told me/him/her'); without an object, use 'said'.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: He said, 'I am learning French.'
options: He said that he was learning French.
He said that he is learning French.
He told that he was learning French.
He said that I was learning French.
practice.explanation: 'said' retained (no object); 'I' → 'he'; Present Continuous 'am learning' → Past Continuous 'was learning'; conjunction 'that' added.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: She said to him, 'You must work hard.'
options: She told him that he must work hard.
She told him that you must work hard.
She said him that he had to work hard.
She told him that he had to work hard.
practice.explanation: 'say to him' → 'told him'; 'you' → 'he' (object rule); 'must' (obligation) → 'had to' in reported speech past context.

practice.question: Change to Indirect Speech: They said, 'We went to Lahore yesterday.'
